Oil Grimoire

Creative Blending

Blending essential oils sits between two impulses: the medical and the aesthetic. In practice these are not separate categories but two ends of the same scale. At one end is therapeutic action on a physical condition like backache. At the other is the emotional or aesthetic response to a particular scent. The person nursing lumbago also carries a temperament and an emotional state, conscious or not, that responds in its own subtle way to a chosen blend. The reverse is also true: a personal perfume that captures someone's character through fragrance has a generally remedial effect on the whole person.

This is why fragrance is worth keeping in mind even when blending principally for medicinal effect. A remedy that smells lovely to the person using it is simply more pleasing to apply, and certain combinations clash for personal reasons (a heavily floral blend, for instance, often does not appeal to men). Choosing and combining oils remains a matter of personal taste, but the guidelines below cover the most useful ground.

Correct Proportions

For therapeutic use, essential oils are diluted before application to the skin. To make a massage or body oil, mix the chosen essential oil or oils into a light base such as grapeseed or sweet almond oil. The dilution table for common blend sizes lives in How to Use Essential Oils at Home. Other suitable bases include sunflower, hazelnut, safflower, peanut, soya, and corn oil. Mineral oils are best avoided.

Heavier, more nourishing oils can be added in small amounts (up to about 10 per cent) when treating specific conditions. These include jojoba, avocado, peach or apricot kernel, borage, olive, sesame, evening primrose, and infused oils such as calendula or St John's wort. A small quantity of wheatgerm oil, around 5 per cent, helps preserve the blend.

The essential oil content in a finished blend usually sits between 1 and 3 per cent, depending on what is being addressed. Physical complaints generally call for a stronger concentration than emotional or nervous conditions. A few oils, the high-quality florals such as rose and jasmine in particular, have unusually strong diffusive power, so a very small percentage is enough to have real effect or to set the character of an entire blend.

Synergies

The proportions of each oil in a blend matter as much as the oils themselves. Some oils, when combined, enhance each other so that the whole is greater than the sum of the parts. The anti-inflammatory action of chamomile, for example, is supported by lavender. A combination working in this kind of harmony is called a synergy. A good synergy takes into account not only the symptom but also the underlying cause of the disorder, the biological terrain of the person, and the psychological or emotional factors at play.

This was the principle behind the Individual Prescription that Marguerite Maury developed for her clients, in which the blend was matched both to physical needs and to circumstance and temperament.

In general, oils from the same botanical family blend well, as do oils that share common constituents. The camphoraceous oils that contain a good proportion of cineol, for instance, work easily together. This group includes the entire Myrtaceae family (eucalyptus, tea tree, cajeput, myrtle, and others) along with many herbs such as spike lavender, rosemary, and Spanish sage. Most floral fragrances pair well with each other, as do the woods, balsams, citruses, and spices. Rosewood and linaloe combine beautifully despite belonging to different families, because both carry a high proportion of linalol and linalyl acetate.

A handful of oils, among them rose, jasmine, oakmoss, and lavender, seem to enhance almost any blend, which is why they appear (often in adulterated form) in most commercial perfumes. The old saying among perfumers is no perfume without rose.

Other combinations work against each other. Oils dominated by aldehydes, such as citronella with its citronellal, those dominated by ketones, such as sage with its thujone, and those rich in phenols, such as clove with its eugenol, tend to pull in different directions when paired together. Knowing the precise chemistry of each oil is not necessary for building a good synergy. Much of it comes down to learning the character of each oil and trusting intuition.

Fragrant Harmony

In the nineteenth century, the Frenchman Piesse introduced a new approach to perfumery by classifying scents according to the notes of a musical scale. He carried the idea of musical harmony into fragrance, treating each scent as a note that, when properly combined with others, formed a balanced chord. The strict version of his theory has long since fallen away, but it still informs perfumery in the form of top, middle, and base notes.

A top note is fresh and light, immediately apparent because of its rapid evaporation rate.

A middle note is the heart of the fragrance and usually forms the bulk of the blend. Its scent emerges shortly after the first impression.

A base note is rich and heavy, emerging slowly and lingering on the skin. It also acts as a fixative, slowing the dispersal of the lighter oils.

Ylang ylang is often described as a well-balanced perfume oil in its own right, with a powerful sweet-floral top, a creamy middle, and a soft, slightly spicy base.

For the sake of simplicity, each essential oil is usually placed into one of these three categories according to its dominant character. Opinions differ, and the list below is meant only as a general orientation.

NoteExamples
Top notestea tree, eucalyptus, mandarin, lemon, basil
Middle notesgeranium, lavender, marjoram, rosewood, rosemary
Base notespatchouli, rose, jasmine, benzoin, frankincense, myrrh

A well-balanced perfume contains elements from all three categories, with the proportions deciding whether the result reads as a heavy oriental scent or a light floral. The same principle applies to aromatherapy work and to personalised remedies.

Oil Grimoire

How to Use Essential Oils at Home

Essential oils can be used simply and effectively at home in a wide range of ways, both for their scent and for their cosmetic and medicinal qualities. They work as perfumes and as refreshers for pot pourris, they can be added to the bath, and they form the basis for personal beauty preparations. They are also useful in minor first aid and in the prevention and relief of common complaints such as headaches, colds, period pains, and aching muscles.

Storage matters. Essential oils should always be kept in a cool place, in dark bottles, with as little contact with air as possible to protect them from photo-oxidation. They should also be kept well out of reach of children.

The methods below cover the most useful ways to apply essential oils at home, with notes on the conditions and oils each method suits best.

Massage

Massage is the method favoured by professional aromatherapists, who usually carry out a full body treatment. Specific essential oils are chosen to suit the condition and temperament of the person being treated, then blended with a base oil such as sweet almond oil or grapeseed oil.

The essential oil content in a blend is usually between 1 and 3 per cent, depending on what is being addressed. As a rough guide, physical complaints such as rheumatism or indigestion call for a stronger concentration than emotional or nervous conditions. A useful conversion is that 20 drops of essential oil equals roughly one millilitre, so the proportions below cover the common blend sizes.

Base oilEssential oil
100 ml20 to 60 drops
25 ml7 to 25 drops
1 tsp3 to 5 drops

Massage is a relaxing and nourishing experience in its own right, in part because of the unspoken communication that touch carries, and in part because it ensures the oils are effectively absorbed through the skin and into the bloodstream. For general well-being it is worth practising self-massage on specific areas of the body, focusing especially on the feet and hands. Targeted rubbing can also help with discomfort. Peppermint, in dilution, can be rubbed on the stomach in a clockwise direction to ease indigestion. Marjoram can help relax a stiff neck and shoulders.

Skin Oils and Lotions

For skin oils and lotions, the preparation follows the same approach as a massage blend, except that the base should include more nourishing oils such as jojoba, avocado, or apricot kernel oil. The emphasis here is on treating the skin itself and tackling specific complaints. Gentle circular finger movements are usually enough for the oils to be absorbed. It is important not to drag the skin, especially around the neck and the eyes. Rose and neroli suit dry or mature complexions. Geranium, bergamot, and lemon help with acne and greasy skin.

A few drops of essential oil can also be mixed into a bland cream or lotion, or added to a face mask built around oatmeal, honey, or clay with the pulp of various fruits. For some conditions, such as cold sores (herpes) and athlete's foot, an alcohol-based lotion works better than an oil or cream. This can be made by adding 6 drops of essential oil to 5 ml of isopropyl alcohol or vodka. The same mixture can be diluted further into a litre of boiled and cooled water for use on open cuts or sores, including those from chickenpox or genital herpes.

Hot and Cold Compresses

Compresses are a simple and very effective way to use essential oils for pain relief and to reduce inflammation.

A hot compress is made by filling a bowl with very hot water and adding 4 or 5 drops of essential oil. Fold a piece of cotton cloth, cotton wool, or a flannel, dip it into the bowl, squeeze out the excess water, and place it on the affected area until it has cooled to blood heat, then repeat. Hot compresses are particularly useful for backache, rheumatism, arthritis, abscesses, earache, and toothache.

A cold compress is made the same way, using ice-cold water in place of hot. This type works well for headaches (apply to the forehead or the back of the neck), sprains, strains, and other hot, swollen conditions.

Hair Care

A few drops of essential oil added to a final hair rinse, or stirred into a mild shampoo, can support hair and scalp health. An alcohol-based scalp rub can be made by adding 5 ml of essential oil to 100 ml of vodka, useful both as a conditioning treatment and for clearing parasites such as lice and fleas.

A deeper conditioning treatment can be made by combining about 3 per cent (around 60 drops) of essential oil with a nourishing base such as olive oil mixed with jojoba or sweet almond oil. Massage this into the scalp and wrap the hair in warm towels for an hour or two. Rosemary, West Indian bay, and chamomile help condition the hair and encourage healthy growth. Lavender repels lice and fleas. Bergamot and tea tree are useful for controlling dandruff.

Flower Waters

A toilet or flower water can be made at home by adding about 20 to 30 drops of essential oil to a 100 ml bottle of spring or de-ionised water. Leave the bottle in the dark for a few days, then filter the water through coffee filter paper. Essential oils do not dissolve in water, but they readily lend it their scent and their properties.

Flower waters are particularly helpful in the prevention and treatment of skin conditions such as acne, dermatitis, and eczema, as well as for general toning and cleansing. Almost any oil can be used. Traditional choices include rose, orange blossom, lavender, and petitgrain. Blended flower waters can also be tailored to suit specific complexions.

Baths

One of the simplest and most pleasurable ways to use essential oils is to add 5 to 10 drops to the bath when the tub is full. Aromatic bathing has a long tradition as a sensual and enjoyable experience, with the Romans among its great enthusiasts, and as a treatment for a wide range of complaints including irritating skin conditions, muscular aches and pains, rheumatism, and arthritis. Ylang ylang offers a euphoric aromatic experience in its own right. Chamomile and lavender ease stress-related complaints such as anxiety and insomnia. Rosemary and pine soothe aching limbs. Take care to avoid oils that may irritate the skin.

Vaporization

A burner or aromatic diffuser is a clean way to scent a room, with none of the dust or smoke that incense produces. A few drops of oil placed on a light bulb ring, or added to a small bowl of water on a radiator, work just as well. Specific oils can be chosen to set different atmospheres. Frankincense and cedarwood have a long ritual history and create a peaceful, relaxed mood. Vaporised citronella or lemongrass keep insects at bay and clear the air of unwanted smells like cigarette smoke.

In earlier times, juniper and rosemary leaves were burned to help control epidemics and purify the air. The same oils can keep an environment free of germs and inhibit the spread of infections like colds and flu. Myrtle or eucalyptus can be vaporised in the bedroom at night to ease breathing difficulties or children's coughs. A few drops on a pillow or a handkerchief carry the same effect through the day.

Always place the burner in a safe spot, well out of reach of children and pets.

Steam Inhalation

Steam inhalation is particularly suited to sinus, throat, and chest infections. Add around 5 drops of an oil such as peppermint or thyme to a bowl of hot water, cover the head and bowl with a towel, and breathe deeply for a minute, then repeat. Sitting in a steaming hot bath is another way to take in a small amount of essential oil through the air, though the dose is far less concentrated. The same approach can serve as a facial sauna: oils like lemon or tea tree help unclog the pores and clear the complexion.

Douche

A douche can help with common genito-urinary infections such as thrush, cystitis, and pruritis. For candida or thrush, add between 5 and 10 drops of tea tree to a litre of warm water and shake well. The mixture can be used in a sitz bath or bidet, or placed in an enema or douche pot, which can be bought from some chemists. Lavender and cypress can also support healing after childbirth.

Neat Application

As a general rule, essential oils are not applied to the skin undiluted, but there are a few notable exceptions. Lavender can be applied neat to burns, cuts, and insect bites. Tea tree can be dabbed on spots. Lemon can be used directly on warts. Sandalwood, jasmine, and rose make excellent perfumes when dabbed neat onto the skin.

Take care with oils that are known to cause skin reactions: phototoxic oils such as bergamot, which discolour the skin when exposed to direct sunlight; irritants such as red thyme; and skin sensitisers such as cinnamon bark.

Blending a selection of oils into a personal fragrance is also worth exploring. Certain oils make excellent additions to linen and clothes, or for refreshing pot pourris. Patchouli, for example, has been used for centuries in India to scent cloth.

Internal Use

Essential oils should not be taken internally at home. They are highly concentrated, and a handful of essences are genuinely toxic. The International Federation of Aromatherapists advises against oral use as well.

This is rarely a practical limitation, because essential oils are absorbed readily through the skin and so reach the internal organs and systems through external application. In a condition like arthritis, which reflects a build-up of toxins in the joints, dietary changes and herbal remedies can be supported externally by oils such as juniper and white birch, which help purify the system while easing pain and inflammation at the site of the swelling.

⚠️
Essential oils should never be used at home to treat serious medical or psychological problems.

Herbal Preparations

These methods apply to herb-based preparations made at home using dried or fresh plant material, without essential oils.

Creams

An unscented, hypoallergenic cream base serves as the carrier. Empty the jar into the top of a double boiler and heat over boiling water. Add the chosen herbs (rose, chamomile, violet, or others) and simmer gently for two hours with the lid on. Use roughly one ounce of dried herbs or two and a half ounces of fresh herbs per ten ounces of cream base. Remove from heat, strain through cheesecloth, and pack into jars with tight-fitting lids. Cool to room temperature before sealing. Store in a cool, dark place.

Decoction

Decoction draws constituents from tough plant materials such as roots and bark. Combine herbs and cold water in a pan, using one ounce of dried herbs or two ounces of fresh herbs per two cups of water. Bring to a boil and simmer gently for twenty to forty minutes, or until the liquid reduces by half to one-third. Strain into a covered container. Store in a cool place or refrigerate. Best used freshly made.

Infusion

An infusion is a strong herbal steep. Use one tablespoon of fresh herbs or two tablespoons of dried herbs per cup of water. For a cold infusion, steep herbs in cold water overnight in a sealed container. For a hot infusion, remove boiling water from heat, add herbs, push them down into the water, cover, and steep for ten minutes. For a sun infusion, place the sealed jar in sunlight and allow the herbs to steep for three to four weeks, shaking daily. Strain and bottle.

Hot Oil Infusion

Combine fresh herbs and a light carrier oil (sunflower, almond, or light olive) in the top of a double boiler. Heat over boiling water for two hours with the lid on. Use one cup of fresh herbs per two cups of oil, or half a cup of dried herbs. Do not allow the oil to boil. Strain through cheesecloth and store in bottles in a cool, dark place. Infused oils serve well for massage, as the base for ointments, or as culinary additions.

Creating Magickal & Perfumed Oils

These instructions apply to perfumed oils, anointing oils, and massage oils blended for magickal use.

Yield Sizes

  • Small batch — 1 to 2 oz · ideal for personal use and anointing candles
  • Large batch — 6 to 8 oz · ideal for massage

How to Blend

  1. Fill your bottle three-quarters full with the carrier oil of your choice — almond, jojoba, or similar.
  2. Add the required drops of essential oil one at a time, using an eye dropper, swirling gently after each addition.
  3. Once all oils are combined, hold the bottle between your hands and focus clearly on the intent you desire, charging the blend with your will.
  4. Cap and label each bottle.
  5. Gently swirl again just before every use to re-integrate the blend.

Dropper Care

Unless the bottle has its own built-in dropper, flush your dropper with rubbing alcohol between each oil — draw it in and push it out several times — to prevent cross-contamination of scents.

Blending for Aromatherapy

When blending for a diffuser rather than for topical use, omit the carrier oil entirely. Drop the essential oils directly into the water in the diffuser container that sits over the heat.

Fixative & Preservation

💧
Add 1 drop of benzoin to every bottle of personal magickal oil — at least 2 drops in massage oils — to act as a fixative and prevent the blend turning rancid. A tiny chip of an appropriate crystal added to the bottle will also amplify and align its energy.

Double-Charging Candle Spells

To add an extra layer of herbal power to candle magick, choose two or three appropriate herbs, grind them finely, spread them on a paper towel, and roll the dressed candle over them so the herbs adhere to the oiled surface.

Testing Essential Oils at Home

Knowing what you're working with matters. Before incorporating an essential oil into your magickal practice, it's worth verifying its purity. Adulterated oils may still carry some energetic properties, but watered-down or chemically altered products won't perform as expected in spellwork or blending.

These two simple at-home tests can reveal whether your essential oils have been diluted, watered down, or treated with additives.

Method 1: The Paper Test

You'll Need: A watercolor paper notebook (available at craft or art supply stores). The thick, absorbent pages prevent oil from bleeding through to subsequent sheets.

Steps

  1. Draw a small shape (circle, square, etc.) to mark your testing area
  2. Record all label information: brand name, botanical (Latin) name, common name, distillation method, lot numbers, batch codes, and any other details
  3. Place a single drop of oil within your marked shape
  4. Allow the oil to air dry naturally without fans or other assistance
  5. Check the paper at one hour, several hours, and again at twenty-four hours
  6. By the final check, the oil should have largely evaporated
  7. Document your observations: Do you see water spots, oily residue, or color stains?

Interpreting Results

Scent: After twenty-four hours, minimal fragrance should remain. Deeper base notes (like vetiver) will linger longer than bright top notes (like orange), but the scent should be faint.

Color: Results vary by source material and extraction method:

  • Distilled citrus oils are typically colorless
  • Expressed citrus oils may leave colored residue (orange oil will stain orange)
  • Root-derived oils like vetiver can be naturally dark
  • Grass-derived oils like lemongrass should be colorless despite the green plant material
⚠️
Red Flag: If your lemongrass or other naturally colorless oil leaves a colored stain, the company has added dyes for aesthetic purposes.

Water spots (tear-stained appearance): The oil has been diluted with water. There's no ethical justification for this practice.

Greasy residue (french-fry-bag appearance): The oil has been cut with carrier oil. Reputable companies disclose dilution and specify which carrier was used, both for allergy safety and budget transparency.

💡
Why Dilution Happens: Some essential oils are extraordinarily expensive due to the time and resources required to produce them. Frankincense, for instance, comes from tree sap that takes roughly twenty years before the tree begins producing. This makes pure frankincense oil cost hundreds of dollars per milliliter. Companies often dilute such oils with carriers like Jojoba Oil, Coconut Oil, or sunflower oil to make them accessible. Ethical vendors clearly state this on the label.

Method 2: The Water Test

You'll Need: A clear container with a lid (a plastic water bottle works well)

Steps

  1. Add approximately 2 oz. of water to the bottle
  2. Add one drop of the essential oil you're testing
  3. Secure the lid tightly and shake vigorously
  4. Observe the contents

Interpreting Results

Cloudy liquid: The oil has been treated with an emulsifier, allowing water to be mixed in.

Oil coating the interior walls: The essential oil has been diluted with carrier oil, whether for cost reduction, profit margins, or other reasons.

Final Thoughts

These tests won't reveal every form of adulteration, but they catch the most common issues. When sourcing oils for magickal work, building relationships with transparent vendors pays dividends. Quality oils carry stronger, cleaner energy and perform more reliably in your practice.

Oil Grimoire

A Guide to Aromatic Materials

Aromatic plants are not interchangeable. The same species grown in two different climates can produce essential oils with quite different characters, and the way an oil is pulled from the plant changes what ends up in the bottle. This guide walks through where these plants grow, the chemistry that gives each oil its action and aroma, and the main extraction methods used to capture them.

Habitat

Roughly thirty plant families and ninety species supply most of the world's essential oils. Spices like allspice, cardamom, clove, nutmeg, and ginger come from tropical regions, while most herbs, including bay, cumin, dill, marjoram, fennel, lavender, rosemary, and thyme, come from temperate climates.

The same plant grown in different soils, altitudes, or weather can yield essential oils of strikingly different makeup. These regional variants are called chemotypes. Common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) is the classic example. Depending on where it grows and which constituent dominates, it may produce a citral or linalol type, a thuyanol type, or a thymol or carvacrol type. Each of these behaves differently on the skin, in the body, and in the nose.

For this reason, the botanical name alone is not enough when sourcing an oil. Place of origin and dominant constituents matter just as much, and reading the chemical profile is one of the main ways quality and purity are confirmed.

Chemistry

Essential oils are built from compounds whose backbone is hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen. They fall into two broad groups: hydrocarbons, made up almost entirely of terpenes (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, and diterpenes), and oxygenated compounds, which include esters, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, phenols, and oxides. Acids, lactones, and traces of sulphur or nitrogen compounds sometimes appear as well.

Terpenes

Common terpene hydrocarbons include limonene, an antiviral that makes up roughly 90 per cent of citrus oils, and pinene, an antiseptic found in high proportions in pine and turpentine oils. Camphene, cadinene, caryophyllene, cedrene, dipentene, phellandrene, terpinene, sabinene, and myrcene also belong to this group. Sesquiterpenes such as chamazulene and farnesol, both present in chamomile, have drawn recent attention for their anti-inflammatory and bactericidal action.

Esters

Esters are probably the most widespread group across essential oils. Linalyl acetate appears in bergamot, clary sage, and lavender, while geranyl acetate appears in sweet marjoram. They tend to be fungicidal and sedative, and often carry a fruity aroma. Bornyl acetate, eugenyl acetate, and lavendulyl acetate are other common esters.

Aldehydes

Citral, citronellal, and neral are the aldehydes most associated with the lemon-scented oils, including melissa, lemongrass, lemon verbena, lemon-scented eucalyptus, and citronella. Aldehydes generally have a sedative effect, and citral in particular has been shown to be antiseptic. Benzaldehyde, cinnamic aldehyde, cuminic aldehyde, and perillaldehyde also belong here.

Ketones

Some of the more notably toxic oil constituents are ketones: thujone in mugwort, tansy, sage, and wormwood, and pulegone in pennyroyal and buchu. That does not make all ketones dangerous. Jasmone in jasmine and fenchone in fennel are non-toxic. Ketones tend to ease congestion and help mucus flow, which is why they often appear in plants used for upper respiratory complaints, such as hyssop and sage. Camphor, carvone, menthone, methyl nonyl ketone, and pinocamphone round out the group.

Alcohols

Alcohols are among the most useful compounds in essential oils. They tend to be antiseptic and antiviral, carry an uplifting quality, and are generally non-toxic. Common terpene alcohols include linalol (in rosewood, linaloe, and lavender), citronellol (in rose, lemon eucalyptus, and geranium), and geraniol (in palmarosa). Borneol, menthol, nerol, terpineol, farnesol, vetiverol, benzyl alcohol, and cedrol fall into this group as well.

Phenols

Phenols are bactericidal and strongly stimulating, but they can also irritate the skin. Eugenol appears in clove and West Indian bay, thymol in thyme, and carvacrol in oregano and savory. Methyl eugenol, methyl chavicol, anethole, safrole, myristicin, and apiol are other common phenols.

Oxides

The most important oxide by far is cineol, also known as eucalyptol, which sits almost in a category of its own. It is expectorant and is the principal constituent of eucalyptus oil. It also appears in many camphoraceous oils such as rosemary, bay laurel, tea tree, and cajeput. Linalol oxide (in decumbent hyssop), ascaridol, bisabolol oxide, and bisabolone oxide are other oxides found in essential oils.

Methods of Extraction

The phrase essential oil is often used loosely to cover anything aromatic pulled from a plant, concretes, resinoids, and absolutes included. Strictly speaking, those products contain only some essential oil along with non-volatile parts like wax or resin, and they are made by different methods, including solvent and carbon dioxide extraction. The aromatic quality of any of these products comes from its essential oil content.

Some plant materials, flowers especially, deteriorate quickly and need to be processed soon after harvest. Others, such as seeds and roots, can be stored or shipped, often to Europe or America, before extraction. The method chosen depends on the plant material itself and the kind of aromatic product being made.

Essential Oils

True essential oils are extracted in two main ways. Citrus oils such as lemon and bergamot are usually obtained by simple expression or pressure. Most others, including lavender, myrrh, sandalwood, and cinnamon, are produced by steam, water, or dry distillation.

Distillation isolates only the volatile, water-insoluble parts of a plant, which means many other valuable constituents like tannins, mucilage, and bitters are left behind. The resulting oil is sometimes redistilled or rectified to remove non-volatile matter. A few oils are redistilled at different temperatures to capture specific constituents and exclude others. Camphor, for example, is split into white, yellow, and brown fractions this way.

Most essential oils are liquid, but some are solid (orris) or semi-solid depending on temperature (rose). They dissolve in pure alcohol, fats, and oils, but not in water. Unlike fixed plant oils such as olive oil, essential oils evaporate when exposed to air and leave no oily residue.

Hydrosols

The water that comes off a steam distillation is not waste. It carries roughly 0.02 to 0.03 per cent dissolved essential oil, which gives it a gentler version of the parent oil's aromatic and energetic character. These aromatic waters are called hydrosols, and they hold the same magickal properties as their corresponding essential oil at a lower price point and a much milder strength.

Hydrosols work well as liquid smudge blends, gentle skin applications, bath additives, room sprays, yoga mat fresheners, and a softer alternative to water diffusers. To build a quick water-based room spray, place 1 teaspoon of table salt or witch hazel in a glass bowl, add 30 drops of essential oil, top with 2 tablespoons of water, and stir well. Transfer to a spray bottle and fill the rest with warm water. Shake before each use.

💧
Note

Always use an intermediary like salt or witch hazel when mixing essential oils with water. Without it the oil will separate and leave stains on whatever the spray lands on.

Concretes

Concretes come almost entirely from plant material such as bark, flower, leaf, herb, or root. Instead of distillation or expression, the material is treated with hydrocarbon-type solvents. This is necessary when the essential oil is harmed by hot water or steam, as with jasmine, and it also yields a more true-to-life fragrance. Some plants, lavender and clary sage among them, are made into either an essential oil by steam distillation or a concrete by solvent extraction. The residue is usually solid and waxy, with no crystalline structure.

Most concretes are about half wax and half volatile oil. Jasmine concrete is typical. In a few cases, like ylang ylang, the concrete is liquid and runs closer to 80 per cent essential oil and 20 per cent wax. Their advantage over pure essential oils is that they are more stable and more concentrated.

Resinoids

Resinoids are made from natural resinous material treated with a hydrocarbon solvent such as petroleum ether or hexane. The key difference from concretes is the source: resinoids come from dead organic material, while concretes come from previously living tissue. Typical sources include balsams (Peru balsam, benzoin), resins (mastic, amber), oleoresins (copaiba balsam, turpentine), and oleo gum resins (frankincense, myrrh).

Resinoids can be viscous liquids, semi-solid, or solid, and are usually homogeneous and non-crystalline. The alcohol-soluble portion of a resinoid is sometimes called an absolute. Frankincense and myrrh can be turned into either an essential oil by steam distillation or a resin absolute by alcohol extraction directly from the crude oleo gum resin. Benzoin is too non-volatile to distill into an essential oil. Liquid benzoin is usually a benzoin resinoid dissolved in a suitable solvent. In perfumery, both concretes and resinoids work as fixatives, prolonging the effect of a fragrance.

Absolutes

An absolute is obtained from a concrete by a second round of solvent extraction, this time using pure ethanol. Wax dissolves only slightly in ethanol, so repeated treatment leaves most of it behind. Even so, some waxes hold on. Orange flower absolute, for example, retains a small amount no matter how thorough the process. Absolutes can then be put through molecular distillation to strip away every remaining trace of non-volatile matter. The alcohol is recovered by evaporation, with a gentle vacuum applied toward the end.

Some absolutes still hold traces of ethanol, around 2 per cent or less, and are not recommended for therapeutic work because of those impurities. Absolutes are usually highly concentrated viscous liquids, though some are solid or semi-solid (clary sage absolute is one). In recent decades, much research has gone into extracting essential oils with liquid carbon dioxide, which produces oils of excellent odour quality with no solvent residues or non-volatile matter to remove.

Pomades

True pomades are the products of enfleurage, a process now nearly obsolete. It was once the main way to capture aromatic material from flowers that kept producing perfume long after they were cut. A glass plate was coated in a thin layer of specially prepared, odourless fat called a chassis. Freshly cut flowers, jasmine or tuberose for example, were laid into the fat one by one, and the fat absorbed their volatile oils. The chassis was renewed with new flowers throughout the harvest. The fragrance-saturated fat that resulted was the pomade, and it was treated with alcohol to produce the pure absolute or perfume.

Natural versus Nature Identical

Many perfumes and oils that were once pulled from flowers like carnation, gardenia, and lilac are now produced almost entirely from synthetics. In the pharmaceutical industry, these chemically constructed products are called nature identical. The perfume and flavouring industries depend on consistency, and naturally grown plants are subject to seasonal variation, which is part of the appeal of a synthetic stand-in. The price tag reflects the difference: synthetic versions are far cheaper than the real thing.

Aromatic oils such as lavender or geranium tend to contain a small number of major constituents, several minor ones, and a very large number of trace elements. Reconstructing that level of complexity, including all the trace elements, is essentially impossible. Most nature identical oils are said to be about 96 per cent accurate, yet it is the remaining 4 per cent, the trace elements, that often define a fragrance's character. Galbanum is a clear case. The pyrazines that give it its powerful green note are present at less than 0.1 per cent of the total oil.

The same principle applies to therapeutic value. The specific blend of constituents in a real essential oil, trace elements included, is what gives it its action. These minute amounts may have a synergistic or controlling effect on the main constituents. Rose contains over 300 different constituents, some still unidentified, which is why synthetic rose oil never quite convinces. Nature identical oils cannot stand in for the natural ones in therapeutic or magickal work. The subtle balance of constituents is lost, and so is the living energy that the plant itself carries.

Recognizing a Good Oil

Price is not a reliable indicator of potency. The most useful approach is to try several brands and learn what a real version of each oil smells, feels, and looks like over time. Ethical suppliers clearly label diluted oils, which is common and expected for the rarer or more expensive varieties.

Some oils are diluted more often than others, either because the pure form is hard to source or because the unblended price would be unreasonable on its own. Frankincense, blue chamomile, jasmine, melissa (lemon balm), myrrh, neroli, and rose are the names to watch most carefully.

Each oil also has tells in its physical character. Vetiver, for instance, should be dark and syrupy. If a bottle is clear and runs thin, it has either been cut or is not really vetiver. Building this kind of recognition takes time and a few side-by-side comparisons, but it is the most reliable shortcut to spotting a fake.

Oil Grimoire

History of Aromatic Oils

Across cultures and centuries, aromatic oils have moved between the temple, the apothecary, and the kitchen. This guide follows that long arc: how essential oils form within plants, why they smell the way they do, and how the earliest civilisations discovered, refined, and ritualised their use, all the way through to the modern practice of aromatherapy and the safety principles that guide it today.

Natural Plant Origins

The distinctive scent and flavour of plants comes from essential oils, the volatile aromatic compounds held within their tissue. These oils are concentrated in tiny pockets and glandular cells, often near the surface, and evaporate easily when exposed to air, infusing the surrounding atmosphere with their characteristic aroma. Citrus is the clearest example. Pressing the peel of an orange releases a visible burst of fragrance, since the oil sits in such profusion just beneath the skin.

Other plants are far more reluctant. The flowers of the rose hold so little aromatic oil that roughly one ton of petals is needed to produce 300g of rose oil. Why some plants generate volatile oils in abundance and others scarcely at all is not fully understood. The aromas appear to draw or repel certain insects and animals, support transpiration and other internal processes, and offer a measure of protection against disease. For these reasons the oils are sometimes described as the hormone or lifeblood of a plant, language that reflects how concentrated and central they are to its living function.

Aromatic oils can be drawn from nearly any part of a plant, including the seeds, bark, root, leaves, flowers, wood, balsam, and resin. A single species often yields several distinct oils depending on the part processed. The bitter orange tree gives three at once: orange oil from the fruit peel, petitgrain from the leaves and twigs, and neroli from the blossoms. The clove tree produces different oils from its buds, stalks, and leaves. The Scotch pine offers separate oils from its needles, wood, and resin. The breadth of aromatic material available from natural sources, and the slow development of techniques for extracting it, reaches back to the heart of the earliest civilisations.

Ancient Civilizations

Aromatic plants and oils have been used for millennia as incense, perfume, cosmetic, medicine, and culinary flavouring. In most early cultures their religious and therapeutic uses were inseparable, and traces of that intertwining remain visible today. Juniper sprigs are still burnt for purification in Tibetan temples, and frankincense continues to be offered during Roman Catholic services.

In the ancient world, perfumes were inseparable from animist and cosmic worldviews. They emerged from ritual practice as fumigations, libations, and ablutions, taking shape first as offerings made during invocations and theophanies before they were treated as instruments of healing.

India

Vedic literature dating to around 2000 BC records over 700 aromatic substances, including cinnamon, spikenard, ginger, myrrh, coriander, and sandalwood. The Indo-Aryan word atar carried multiple meanings at once: smoke, wind, odour, and essence. The Rig Veda treats these substances as both liturgical and therapeutic, and frames the handling of herbs as sacred work performed in partnership with the plants themselves. This body of knowledge developed into the Ayurvedic system of medicine, which has been transmitted in unbroken succession into the present day.

China

Chinese herbalism accompanies the practice of acupuncture and is recorded in the Yellow Emperor's Book of Internal Medicine, which dates to more than 2,000 years BC. Aromatics such as opium and ginger appear among its remedies. The same substances also served religious functions in early ceremonies, including the Li-ki and Tcheou-Li rites. Borneo camphor remains in heavy ritual use across China to this day.

Egypt

Egyptian civilisation carries the richest associations with the earliest aromatic materials. Papyri from the reign of Khufu around 2800 BC list numerous medicinal herbs, and a manuscript from around 2000 BC speaks of fine oils, choice perfumes, and the incense of temples by which every god is gladdened. Cedar and myrrh were used in the embalming process, and traces of scented unguents and oils such as styrax and frankincense have been recovered from ornate jars and cosmetic pots within the tombs. Stone inscriptions along the Nile valley preserve a complete iconography of how these oils, balsams, and fermented liqueurs were prepared.

The Egyptians were renowned cosmetologists. One celebrated remedy, kyphi, combined sixteen ingredients and could be burnt as incense, worn as perfume, or taken internally as medicine. It was considered antiseptic, balsamic, and soothing, regarded as an antidote to poison, and credited with the power to ease anxiety, lull sleepers into rest, and brighten dreams.

Treasures from the East

Natural aromatics and perfume materials were among the earliest trade goods of the ancient world, prized for their rarity and held as treasures. When the Jewish people departed Egypt for Israel around 1240 BC, they carried precious gums and oils with them, along with the knowledge of how to use them. The Book of Exodus records that Moses received the formula for a holy anointing oil during the journey, blended from myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil. This oil was used to consecrate Aaron and his sons into priesthood, a rite passed from one generation to the next. Frankincense and myrrh, both counted among the great treasures of the East, were the gifts offered to the infant Jesus at his birth.

Phoenician merchants moved scented oils and gums outward from the Levant, first across the Arabian peninsula and gradually throughout the Mediterranean, particularly into Greece and Rome. They opened the West to the riches of the Orient, carrying camphor from China, cinnamon from India, gums from Arabia, and rose from Syria, while guarding their trading routes as a closely held secret.

Greeks

The Greeks learnt a great deal from the Egyptians. Herodotus and Democrates, who visited Egypt during the fifth century BC, later transmitted what they had gathered about perfumery and natural therapeutics back to Greek soil. Around 425 BC Herodotus became the first to record a method for distilling turpentine, alongside the earliest detailed accounts of perfumes and the materials that produced them. Dioscorides afterwards compiled a five-volume materia medica known as the Herbarius, which catalogued the sources and uses of the plants and aromatics employed by both the Greeks and the Romans.

Hippocrates, born in Greece about 460 BC and revered as the father of medicine, prescribed perfumed fumigations and fomentations as part of his practice. From Greek medical tradition comes the term iatralypte, naming a physician who healed through aromatic unctions. One celebrated Greek preparation, megaleion, was named for its creator Megallus and combined myrrh, cinnamon, and cassia. Like Egyptian kyphi, it served as both a perfume and a remedy, particularly for skin inflammation and battle wounds.

Romans

The Romans surpassed even the Greeks in their use of perfumes and aromatic oils. Three classes of perfume were in common use: ladysmata, solid unguents; stymmata, scented oils; and diapasmata, powdered perfumes. These were applied to hair, body, clothing, and bedding, and large quantities of scented oil were used for massage after bathing.

Transmission to the Arab World

With the fall of the Roman Empire and the rise of Christianity, many Roman physicians fled to Constantinople, carrying with them the books of Galen, Hippocrates, and Dioscorides. These Graeco-Roman works were translated into Persian, Arabic, and other languages, and by the close of the Byzantine Empire that knowledge had passed into the Arab world. Europe, meanwhile, entered the long stretch known as the Dark Ages.

Alchemy

Between the seventh and thirteenth centuries the Arab world produced a remarkable lineage of scientists, among them Avicenna (AD 980 to 1037). This physician and scholar wrote more than a hundred books in his lifetime, one of which was devoted entirely to the flower most beloved within Islam, the rose. He is credited with the invention of the refrigerated coil, a breakthrough in distillation that allowed the production of pure essential oils and aromatic waters.

The honour of inventing distillation, however, may belong much further back. In 1975 Dr Paolo Rovesti led an archaeological expedition to Pakistan to study the ancient Indus Valley civilisation. In the museum of Taxila, at the foot of the Himalayas, he documented a perfectly preserved distillation apparatus made of terracotta, alongside perfume containers from the same period of around 3000 BC. The presence of both items together suggests that the Arabs were not the originators of the technique but the inheritors of a process already practised more than four thousand years earlier.

Distillation Returns to Europe

Rose water, carried back to the West at the time of the Crusades along with other exotic essences, became one of the most popular scents in Europe. The technique of distillation arrived with it. By the thirteenth century the perfumes of Arabia were famous across the continent. Throughout the Middle Ages, floors were strewn with aromatic plants, and small herbal bouquets were carried as protection against plague and other infectious diseases. Lacking the gum-yielding trees of the Orient, Europeans gradually turned to their native herbs: lavender, sage, and rosemary. By the sixteenth century lavender water and the so-called chymical oils could be purchased from the apothecary. After the invention of printing, the period from 1470 to 1670 saw the publication of many herbals, among them the Grete Herball of 1526, which included illustrations of the retorts and stills used to extract volatile oils.

The Hermetic Pursuit

In the hands of the philosophers, the art of distillation became inseparable from alchemy, the hermetic pursuit dedicated to the transformation of base metals into gold and the gross into the subtle. The work was first and foremost a religious one. The stages of distillation were equated with stages of inner psychic transmutation, a process of dissolution and coagulation: separation (black, lead), extraction (white, quicksilver), fusion (red, sulphur), and finally sublimation (gold, or lapis). Just as aromatic material could be distilled to yield a pure and potent essence, the human emotions could be refined and concentrated to reveal their true nature. Within this framework, volatile oils were understood as the purified psyche, the quintessence of the alchemists, an emanation of matter and a manifestation of spirit, mediating between the two realms.

Alchemy served as the bridge across which the symbolism of the ancient Arab, Greek, and Gnostic worlds was carried into the modern era. As that symbolic language crossed the bridge, it began to be tested in continuous, dynamic interaction with the findings of chemistry.

The Birth of Aromatherapy

The term aromatherapy was first coined in 1928 by the French chemist Gattefossé, who worked in his family's perfumery business. His interest in the therapeutic potential of essential oils began with a workplace accident. After badly burning his hand, he plunged it into the nearest cool liquid, which happened to be lavender oil. The burn healed rapidly and left no scar. Through subsequent investigation he found that essential oils were often more effective in their whole, natural form than as synthetic substitutes or isolated active constituents. Cuthbert Hall had reached a similar conclusion as early as 1904, demonstrating that the antiseptic strength of eucalyptus oil was greater than that of its main isolated component, eucalyptol, also called cineol.

The French physician Dr Jean Valnet incorporated essential oils into his medical and psychiatric practice, treating specific disorders with them. His findings appeared in 1964 under the title Aromatherapie. Valnet's work was studied in turn by Madame Marguerite Maury, who applied his research to beauty therapy. Maury sought to revitalise her clients by formulating a strictly personal aromatic complex tailored to each person's temperament and particular health concerns, treating perfumed essences as medicinal agents rather than purely aesthetic ones.

Beyond Scent

The word aromatherapy can mislead, since it implies a healing approach working only through smell and emotion. In practice, each essential oil carries an individual combination of constituents that interacts directly with the body's chemistry, affecting specific organs and systems as a whole. When applied externally during massage, oils are absorbed through the skin and transported throughout the body. A simple demonstration is to rub a clove of garlic on the soles of the feet. Its volatile oil enters the bloodstream and a short time later the odour appears on the breath.

Three Modes of Action

Essential oils interact with the human body in three distinct ways.

The pharmacological mode covers the chemical changes that occur when an oil enters the bloodstream and reacts with hormones, enzymes, and other biological agents.

The physiological mode addresses how an oil affects the body's systems, whether sedating, stimulating, or otherwise altering function.

The psychological mode involves the response to a scent on inhalation, the emotional and mental reaction to odour itself.

The first two modes place aromatherapy in close company with medical herbalism, or phytotherapy. The aroma matters, but so does the chemical interaction between the oils and the body and the physical changes that result.

Herbal Medicine

The practice of aromatherapy can be understood as one branch of the larger field of herbal medicine, since an essential oil is only one of many forms in which a plant can be prepared as a remedy. Because every essential oil is derived directly from a plant, it benefits from being seen within a broader botanical context rather than treated as an isolated product. Aromatherapy and herbal medicine are not synonymous, but complementary.

Most plants that yield essential oils are also used in medical herbalism, but the therapeutic qualities of an oil must be distinguished from those of the whole herb or its other preparations.

German Chamomile

German chamomile illustrates this clearly. The herb is widely prepared as an infusion, tincture, or decoction, in addition to being processed for its volatile oil. Chamazulene, a major constituent of the oil, accounts for chamomile's longstanding reputation as a relaxant and soothing skin remedy, owing to its pain-relieving, antispasmodic, wound-healing, and anti-inflammatory activity. The essential oil is well suited to the treatment of nervous conditions, insomnia, and dermal irritation or disease. The whole herb, however, also contains a bitter principle (anthemic acid), tannins (tannic acid), mucilage, and glycosides. Its overall effect emerges from the combined action of all these pharmacologically active constituents, which in chamomile or Matricaria includes the astringency of the tannins and the stimulation of the bitters. In an infusion, tincture, or decoction the volatile oil is less concentrated, the potency of the oil is reduced, and the safety margin is increased, making the herbal preparation better suited to internal use.

Peppermint

Peppermint shows the same pattern. The oil is excellent for respiratory conditions when used as an inhalant, particularly because of its antispasmodic and antiseptic action. For longer term treatment of digestive disorders, however, extracts from the whole herb are preferable, since the volatile oil's action is supported by the presence of bitters and tannins. In herbal medicine the effect of any single herb is also typically reinforced by combining it with others.

Meadowsweet

It is also incorrect to assume that the essential oil is always the most active or therapeutically valuable part of a plant. Meadowsweet contains an essential oil of remarkable antiseptic strength: 3.3cc of meadowsweet essence renders infertile 1000cc of microbic cultures in sewage, compared to 5.6cc of phenol for the same volume. Even so, the plant also yields salicylic glycosides, valued for their pain-relieving and anti-inflammatory qualities. Aspirin, derived from salicylic acid, takes its name from the herb's old country name, spiraea.

Almond

The almond tree offers another example. The kernels of both the bitter and sweet almond trees are used to produce a fixed oil, commonly known as sweet almond oil, which has many cosmetic applications. The kernels of the bitter almond tree are also used to produce the essential oil that gives marzipan its characteristic flavour, but in unrefined form they contain cyanide. The properties of a plant, even the same part of a plant, can differ greatly depending on how it is prepared.

Therapeutic Guidelines

The accepted code of practice in modern aromatherapy is to use essential oils as external remedies only. This guidance reflects the high concentration of the oils and the irritation or damage they can cause to the mucous membranes and the delicate lining of the stomach when applied undiluted. There appears to be a kind of natural fit in this approach. Volatile oils mix readily with the carrier oils and ointments suited to external application, are absorbed easily through the skin, and vaporise readily for inhalation. When inhaled, they affect mood and feeling while at the same time producing physiological changes throughout the body. A Japanese experiment carried out in 1963 found that the effects of essential oils on the digestive system were likely to be stronger when the oils were inhaled than when they were ingested.

Herbs, by contrast, yield up many of their qualities to water and alcohol, which makes them appropriate for internal use. They lack the concentrated aromatic element, however, and so do not produce the same subtle effects on the mind and emotions.

Exceptions and Edge Cases

These are only general guidelines, and there are exceptions. Plantain is an excellent wound-healing herb valuable for external use, yet it contains no essential oil. A great many aromatic oils are also used to flavour food and drink and are consumed daily in minute amounts. Peppermint oil appears in a wide range of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages, confectionery, and prepared savoury foods, with the highest average use staying at or below 0.104 per cent. The mint oils, including spearmint and cornmint, are used extensively in the pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries, appearing in toothpaste, cough and cold remedies, soaps, creams, lotions, colognes, and perfumes. Cornmint also serves as the starting material for the production of menthol used in the drug industry.

A Wide and Varied Spectrum

The use of essential oils therefore covers a wide and varied spectrum. They share the holistic qualities of natural plant remedies, although some herbalists view them in much the same light as synthetic drugs, treating an essential oil as a part of the whole rather than the whole herb itself. At the same time they play an active role in modern pharmaceutical manufacture, both in their full form and as isolated constituents such as phenol and menthol.

Safety Precautions

This section provides general safety guidance for the use of essential oils. It is not a substitute for the specific safety profile of any individual oil.

Safety Data

Always consult the safety profile of a new oil before use, with particular attention to toxicity, phototoxicity, dermal irritation, and sensitisation.

Contra-indications

Note all contra-indications listed for a given oil. Common examples:

  • Fennel, hyssop, and sage should be avoided by anyone with epilepsy
  • Clary sage should not be used while drinking alcohol
  • Hops should not be used by anyone suffering from depression

High Blood Pressure

Avoid the following oils in cases of high blood pressure: hyssop, rosemary, sage (all types), and thyme.

Homoeopathy

Homoeopathic treatment is not compatible with the following oils: black pepper, camphor, eucalyptus, and the mint oils.

Pregnancy

During pregnancy, use essential oils at half the usual stated amount, and observe all oils that are contra-indicated for pregnancy.

Babies and Children

Use with care, in accordance with age.

AgeDosage
Babies (0 to 12 months)1 drop of lavender, rose, chamomile, or mandarin diluted in 1 tsp of base oil for massage or bathing
Infants (1 to 5 years)2 to 3 drops of safe essential oils (non-toxic and non-irritant to the skin) diluted in 1 tsp of base oil for massage or bathing
Children (6 to 12 years)As for adults, but in half the stated amount
Teenagers (over 12 years)As directed for adults

Types of Oils

Base & Carrier Oils

What Are Base and Carrier Oils?

Base oils and carrier oils are interchangeable terms for the same thing in essential oil work. These oils enhance magickal effects and typically come from seeds or nuts. The energy of new life within seeds and nuts brings a powerful push of creation to any spell.

Recommended Dilution

Here are some general rules of thumb for when you're mixing an essential oil with a carrier oil:

1% dilution or less: Delicate skin areas, around the eyes and face; oils that are safe to use during pregnancy

1.5% dilution: Emotional aromatherapy, energy work

2.5% dilution: Massage therapy, general aromatherapy, skincare for thicker skin (elbows, feet)

The recipes in this book are calculated for 2.5% for skin safety and 0.5% with sensitizing oils like cinnamon. There are websites and smartphone apps that include dilution calculators. Above 2.5% is not recommended for magickal aromatherapy. Discuss with a certified aromatherapist, massage therapist, or naturopath before using.

Choosing a Carrier Oil

When selecting a carrier oil, consider:

  • Situation or occasion: Match the oil to your working
  • Shelf life: Short-lived oils for immediate use, longer-lasting oils for storage
  • Personal preference: Choose oils you resonate with

For sabbat oils used by a small group, choose oils with longer shelf life and blend small amounts. For large gatherings where oil will be used immediately, shorter shelf life oils work well.

Extending Shelf Life

Orifice Reducers

Orifice reducers prevent spills and keep oils fresher longer by limiting oxygen exposure.

Preservatives

Vitamin E: Best for massage oils. Add 10 drops vitamin E per 8 fluid ounces of carrier oil.

Tincture of Benzoin: Add 5 drops per ounce of carrier oil.

To make benzoin tincture: Mix ¼ teaspoon ground benzoin with ¼ cup 100-proof vodka. Shake vigorously and steep for six weeks.

Proper Storage

Store oils in dark glass or dark PET plastic bottles away from UV rays. Maintain a stable, cool temperature. Heat is as damaging as light exposure.

Oils with short shelf life can be refrigerated to extend their lifespan. Label blends with expiration dates. Trust your nose, you'll recognize rancid oil immediately.

Remember: Even in dark storage, oils oxidize. The more oil used from a bottle, the more oxygen enters, accelerating deterioration.

Infused & Conditioned Oils

Infused oils are made by placing herbal material into the chosen carrier oil and allowing the oil to take on the properties of the plant material over time. Let the mixture sit in a dark corner cabinet or on a shelf in a warm room for a few weeks. The oil will take on the properties of the plant material. Infused oils are much less fragrant than essential oils but can be used effectively in magick and may be significantly more cost-effective.

Tips for Crafting Infused Oils

  • Dried material is always used to prevent molding.
  • The key to infused oils is patience.
  • With harder, woody plant material, the infused oil may not be ready to use for six to eight weeks.
  • If you are making an oil for a special occasion, make sure to leave plenty of time.

Benefits of Making Your Own Infused Oils

The benefit of making your own infused oils is that you can use plant materials that are rare, that are not available in essential oil form, or that are too sensitizing for cosmetic use but may be suitable for magickal use. Plants that have no cosmetic or holistic usefulness can be infused to use year-round. The oils that are locked in the plant material will then be absorbed into the fatty oils of the carrier that is being used.

Examples in Practice

Many cooking oils employ this technique. For example, olive oil infused with Chinese hot peppers is frequently available at the grocery store. It carries properties of the Chinese hot pepper and is similarly useful for banishing spells.

This technique is also beneficial for plants that in essential oil form would be ill suited, too sensitizing for use on skin, or irritating in ritual baths. A practitioner could choose to break up several bay leaves and place them in a carrier oil to make an infused oil for communication, a protection bath oil, or a candle oil for love spells.

Purple dead nettle (Lamium purpureum) grows wild all over North America in poor soil and on the side of the road. This tempestuous "weed" (remember, "weed" just means a plant that grows where it is not intended to) is valuable for use in spells involving joy and happiness. While it has no smell, and is not suited to essential oil production, an infused oil is the perfect use for this herb. Simply dry plant material and add to a carrier oil.

Dried plant material is more suited to infused oils, as water content can lead to reduced shelf life or spoiling concerns. For harder, heartier, or woody plant material, look to conditioned oils.

Basic Recipe for an Infused Oil

  1. Fill a 4-ounce bottle halfway with carrier oil.
  2. Place 2 tablespoons of dried plant material in the bottle and fill the rest of the way with carrier oil. Do not forget to leave room in the headspace for a dropper, if your bottle has one. Placing the herbs in the middle of the bottle makes the mixture easier to stir.
  3. Shake the bottle daily for the first week, and let it sit for a minimum of six weeks before use.

Jojoba is a great choice for infused oils, as it is shelf stable for up to two years or more, when properly stored. You'll know if it goes rancid. Your nose will alert you. Rancid jojoba smells like burnt gym socks. If this should happen, just throw it away. There is no trick to save it. Dispose of it and get a new, fresh supply.

Conditioned Oils

Conditioned oils are similar to infused oils, with two key differences: the use of fresh plants and low heat. The application of heat removes excess water from the mixture, so fresh plant material can be used. Conditioned oils may have a stronger fragrance and a bit more energy than their infused counterparts. All that energy goes into your magickal working.

With the advent of slow cookers and crockpot liners, creating personalized oils is much easier. Have the slow cooker on "keep warm" or low heat for conditioning oils, even overnight. The key is to keep the mixture at low heat because you don't want to damage the volatile oils in the plant material. Anytime there are plant materials present, make sure the lid is on tightly. After eight hours or so, turn off the heat and allow the oil to cool. Then bottle; no need to sit before use.

Bath Oils

Cost-effective and naturally scented, bath oils are a major player in the list of oil tricks. They can be given as gifts at holidays and put together on the go after a stressful day.

Place 5 to 7 drops of essential oil into 1 ounce of carrier oil. This blend will nourish skin and leave you feeling soft and sweet-smelling. If there is a concern about slipping, consider mixing your essential oil into whole milk or powdered milk, rather than oil, and pour into the bathtub. The milk acts as an emulsifier, allowing the oil to mix with the bathwater. This makes a nice contrast to bath salts, which can have a drying effect on chapped or damaged skin.

Bath Salts

Bath salts are a quick and easy method of dispersing essential oils into bathwater without the dangers of slipping and falling associated with bath oils. Magickally, salt is purifying and beneficial for aching muscles and many other health and well-being challenges.

Sugar Scrubs

Sugar scrubs can be enjoyed in the shower, but remember never to add sugar to bathwater. Sugar added to bathwater can feed yeast organisms and lead to an overgrowth, known as an infection.

Sugar Scrubs vs. Salt Scrubs

Salt and sugar may look similar, but that's where the similarities end. When it comes to the types of skin on the body, the thicker skin (hands, arms, legs, feet) will benefit from a sugar scrub over a salt scrub. The salt scrub will feel softer on the face and will not have the sharp edges that sugar crystals do. On thinner facial skin, the edges of sugar crystals can lead to micro lacerations that can become infected and lead to scarring and premature aging.

Ajowan

Steam distillation of the greyish-brown seeds of Ajowan yields a yellow-orange to reddish liquid with a herbaceous-spicy, medicinal scent that reads very much like thyme. Its principal constituents include thymol, pinene, cymene, dipentene, terpinene, and carvacrol, among others. Its dominant actions are powerful antiseptic and germicide, with carminative qualities as well.

Traditional Use

In Indian medicine, the tincture, essential oil, and isolated thymol have all been put to use, with cholera among the conditions traditionally treated.

Other Uses

Historically, ajowan was a major source for the isolation of thymol, though that role has largely been taken over by synthetic thymol production.

Almond

Bitter almond essential oil is steam-distilled from the kernels of the bitter variety of Almond. The nuts are pressed and macerated in warm water for twelve to twenty-four hours before distillation, and prussic acid forms during that maceration. The raw seed contains none. Most commercial bitter almond oil is rectified to remove the acid and is labelled FFPA, free from prussic acid. The rectified product is a light, colourless liquid carrying the characteristic marzipan scent that gives the oil its commercial value.

Its principal constituents are benzaldehyde at around 95 per cent and prussic acid at around 3 per cent. Prussic acid, also called hydrocyanic acid, is cyanide. Benzaldehyde is itself moderately toxic. For these reasons, the oil is not suitable for therapeutic use in any form, internal or external, even after rectification.

Other Uses

Bitter almond oil is no longer used in internal medicine. The rectified version flavours foods, mostly confectionery, where almond essence and marzipan are the most common applications. In food flavouring it is increasingly being replaced by synthetic benzaldehyde.

Botanical family: Cupressaceae

Origin: Mediterranean region

Source: Needles and twigs

Magickal Uses

Cypress excels in blessing and consecrating ritual tools, spaces, and objects. Add to anointing oils for dedication ceremonies.

Use in protective blends to create strong boundaries. Cypress guards against negative influences while maintaining connection to ancestral wisdom.

Particularly suited for emotional healing work, especially around grief, loss, and transformation. Diffuse during times of mourning or major life transitions.

The tree's association with cemeteries and eternal life makes cypress oil valuable for work involving ancestors, death acceptance, and finding peace in endings.

Blending

Cypress blends well with patchouli (as in the Ambergris Bouquet substitute), lavender, sandalwood, and other woody or earthy oils.

Spellwork Correspondences

Rub oil from center to either end to dress the candle, from top to bottom to draw energy toward you, or bottom to top to banish. Oils are flammable; use with care. Spellwork uses include calmative, soothes emotions, stability, and the Underworld.

Extraction & Characteristics

The essential oil is steam-distilled from the needles and twigs. An oil from the cones is occasionally available, and small quantities of concrete and absolute are also produced. The oil is a pale yellow to greenish-olive mobile liquid with a smoky, sweet-balsamic, tenacious odour. Principal constituents include pinene, camphene, sylvestrene, cymene, and sabinol, among others.

Related Species

Many other species of cypress worldwide are used to produce essential oils, including C. lusitanica from Kenya. With regard to oil quality, C. sempervirens is considered superior.

Folk Tradition

Ancient civilizations valued cypress as both a medicine and an incense, and Tibetans still use it as a purification incense. It benefits the urinary system and is considered useful where there is excessive loss of fluid, including heavy perspiration, menstrual loss, and diarrhoea. The cones were noted as very drying and binding, useful for stopping fluxes of all kinds. Chinese tradition considers the nuts nutritious, beneficial for the liver and respiratory system, and helpful for checking profuse perspiration.

Therapeutic Uses

In skin care, cypress addresses haemorrhoids, oily and overhydrated skin, excessive perspiration, varicose veins, wounds, and pyorrhoea (bleeding of the gums), and serves as an insect repellent. For circulation, muscles, and joints, it works on cellulitis, muscular cramp, oedema, poor circulation, and rheumatism. In the respiratory system, it addresses asthma, bronchitis, and spasmodic coughing. In the genito-urinary system, it eases dysmenorrhoea, menopausal problems, and menorrhagia. For the nervous system, it supports nervous tension and stress-related conditions.

Full Blending Profile

Cypress blends well with cedarwood, Pine Essential Oil, Lavender Essential Oil, mandarin, Clary Sage Essential Oil, Lemon Essential Oil, Cardamom Essential Oil, Moroccan Chamomile Essential Oil, Ambrette Seed Essential Oil, labdanum, Juniper Berry Essential Oil, Benzoin Absolute, Bergamot Essential Oil, Orange Essential Oil, Marjoram Essential Oil, and Sandalwood Essential Oil.

Safety

Galbanum Essential Oil is steam- or water-distilled from the oleoresin of Ferula galbaniflua, a large perennial herb of the Mediterranean and Middle East whose stems exude a milky natural oleoresin. Only the Levant or soft type of galbanum is used for oil production; the harder Persian variety is reserved for resinoid and pharmaceutical work.

Botanical Information

  • Scientific name: Ferula galbaniflua (also classified as F. gummosa)
  • Family: Apiaceae (Umbelliferae)
  • Plant: Large perennial herb with a smooth stem, shiny leaflets, and small flowers. Resin ducts within the stem exude a milky oleoresin.
  • Source of oil: Dried oleoresinous exudation, collected by incising the base of the stem
  • Evaporation: Top to middle note (fresh green topnote with a balsamic undertone)

Distribution

Native to the Middle East and western Asia. Cultivated in Iran, Turkey, Afghanistan, and Lebanon. Distillation usually takes place in Europe or the USA.

Other Species and Forms

Galbanum exists in two distinct commercial types: Levant galbanum, which is liquid or soft and used for essential oil production, and Persian galbanum, which is solid or hard and reserved for resinoid and pharmaceutical preparation. Other Ferula species also yield galbanum-like gum, including the muskroot. The closely related Zalou root (F. hermonic) is used in Beirut as an aphrodisiac.

Extraction & Characteristics

Method: Water or steam distillation from the oleoresin or gum (Levant type only). A partially deterpenised oil known as "galbanol" is also produced, and a resinoid is prepared mainly for use as a fixative.

Crude oleoresin: A dark amber or brown viscous liquid with a green-woody scent and soft balsamic undertone.

Distilled oil: A colourless, pale yellow, or olive liquid carrying a fresh green topnote and woody-dry balsamic undertone.

Principal Constituents

Pinene, cadinol, cadinene, and myrcene, among others.

Safety

Non-toxic, non-irritant, and non-sensitising.

Therapeutic Actions

Analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antiseptic, antispasmodic, aphrodisiac, balsamic, carminative, cicatrisant, digestive, diuretic, emmenagogue, expectorant, hypotensive, restorative, and tonic.

Folk and Historical Use

Used by the ancient civilisations as a ceremonial incense, in Egyptian cosmetics, and in the embalming process. Eastern herbalism has long employed galbanum in much the same way as asafetida: for wounds, inflammations, and skin disorders, and for respiratory, digestive, and nervous complaints.

Aromatherapy Uses

  • Skin care: abscesses, acne, boils, cuts, scar tissue, inflammations, skin toning, mature skin, wrinkles, wounds; the oil "signifies drying and preservation."
  • Circulation, muscles, and joints: poor circulation, muscular aches and pains, rheumatism.
  • Respiratory system: asthma, bronchitis, catarrh, chronic coughs.
  • Digestive system: cramp, flatulence, indigestion.
  • Nervous system: nervous tension and stress-related complaints.

Source-Named Blending Partners

Hyacinth Absolute, Violet Leaf Absolute, Narcissus Oil, Lavender Essential Oil, Geranium Essential Oil, Oakmoss Absolute, opopanax, Pine Essential Oil, Fir Needle Essential Oil, Levant Storax Essential Oil, and oriental bases.

Other Uses

The Persian gum was historically employed in pharmaceutical products. Both oil and resinoid serve as fixatives and fragrance components in soaps, detergents, creams, lotions, and perfumes. Galbanum also appears as a flavour ingredient across most major food categories and in alcoholic and soft drinks.

Levant Storax Essential Oil, also called Styrax, is steam-distilled from the balsamic exudate of Storax (Liquidambar orientalis), the oriental sweetgum tree of Asia Minor. The oil shares similar qualities with Benzoin Absolute, which is produced from the related Styrax benzoin.

Extraction & Characteristics

The essential oil is produced by steam distillation from the crude balsam, which is itself a pathological secretion induced by pounding the bark of the tree. A resinoid and an absolute are also produced from the crude by solvent extraction. The finished oil is a water-white or pale yellow liquid with a sweet-balsamic, rich, tenacious odour. Principal constituents are mainly styrene, with vanillin, phenylpropyl alcohol, cinnamic alcohol, benzyl alcohol, and ethyl alcohol, among others.

Therapeutic Uses

Storax is recorded as anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antiseptic, antitussive, bactericidal, balsamic, expectorant, nervine, and stimulant. In aromatherapy and home use, the oil is applied to skin care for cuts, ringworm, scabies, and wounds; to the respiratory system for bronchitis, catarrh, and coughs; and to the nervous system for anxiety and stress-related conditions.

Blending

The oil blends well with Ylang Ylang Essential Oil, Jasmine Absolute, Mimosa Absolute, Rose Oil, Lavender Essential Oil, Carnation Oil, Violet Leaf Absolute, Cassie Absolute, and spice oils.

Safety

Storax is non-toxic and non-irritant, with possible sensitization in some individuals. The oil is frequently adulterated; low-priced storax oil is usually an imitation rather than the genuine product.

Where You Will Encounter It

Storax is used in compound benzoin tincture, mainly for respiratory conditions. The oil and resinoid are used as fixatives and fragrance components mainly in soaps, floral and oriental perfumes. The resinoid and absolute are used in most major food categories, including alcoholic and soft drinks.

Magickal Uses

Storax has a long history in sacred perfumery. Its resinous depth adds gravitas to ritual blends.

Traditionally used in magickal and religious incenses for its grounding, centering properties.

Substitution

Substitute Benzoin essential oil for storax. While this does not duplicate the fragrance exactly, it can be used in magickal formulas calling for storax. Benzoin Siam is related to storax and makes the closest substitute.

Substitute benzoin siam when storax is unavailable, as they are botanically related. Best fumed on charcoal to release its full aromatic richness.

Scent Profile

Magickal Uses

The rose-like qualities make palmarosa naturally suited for love workings. Add to love blends or dilute and wear to attract romantic attention.
