Plant Grimoire

Herbs in Self-Care

Witches have long served as healers. Long before pharmaceuticals existed, communities turned to cunning folk, alewives, and wise women for remedies rooted in the natural world. Herbs were the foundation of those preparations, and the oldest known written record of medicinal herb use is an ancient Sumerian clay tablet engraved with herbal cures. The plants that brought balance to body, mind, and spirit in those early traditions are still in use today.

This guide explores the major systems of herbal health and how those traditions connect to modern witchcraft practice.

Herbal Systems of Health

Across cultures and centuries, herbs have been woven into formalized systems of healing. Each system carries its own philosophy about what health means and how balance is achieved. Understanding these frameworks helps contextualize the plants you work with and the traditions they come from.

Allopathy

Allopathy is the dominant healthcare model in Western society. It works by targeting and reducing specific symptoms rather than treating the whole person. Most allopathic treatments rely on pharmaceutical drugs, and a significant portion of those trace their active ingredients back to plant sources. Roughly 25 percent of all prescription medicines contain compounds originally derived from plants.

These plant-derived compounds are called phytochemicals. When isolated and purified for clinical use, they become part of allopathic medicine. When the whole plant is used instead, this is referred to as phytomedicine.

Many plant-based preparations are sold in the United States as dietary supplements. It is worth noting that "natural" does not mean "safe." Herbal preparations carry real potency, and allergic reactions can develop at any stage of life. Anyone adding herbal supplements to their routine should research potential interactions, contraindications, and side effects carefully, particularly if also taking prescription medications.

Naturopathy

Naturopathy takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than targeting isolated symptoms, naturopathic practitioners work to support the body's own capacity for healing. Treatment is individualized, with remedies and regimens tailored to the specific needs of each person.

Beyond herbs, a naturopath may incorporate dietary changes, exercise, massage, and detoxification practices into a healing plan. In the United States, naturopathic physicians complete a four-year graduate program and must pass licensing examinations before practicing.

This whole-person philosophy aligns closely with the witchcraft tradition of working with plants to support overall balance rather than simply suppressing symptoms.

Homeopathy

Homeopathy operates on the principle that "like cures like": that a substance capable of producing symptoms in a healthy person can, in highly diluted form, stimulate the body to heal those same symptoms. Like naturopathy, homeopathy aims to activate the body's innate healing capacity rather than suppress symptoms directly. Unlike naturopathy, however, homeopathy remains centered on symptoms rather than the whole person.

Remedies are prepared in extremely low concentrations, which makes the practice controversial. Two people presenting the same symptoms may receive entirely different remedies, making efficacy difficult to measure through conventional clinical trials. Some view this as a limitation; others see it as reflecting the same individualized logic that underlies magickal practice, the idea that intention, resonance, and subtle energetics can produce real results beyond what standard measurement captures.

In the United States, homeopathic physicians generally complete a four-year degree, though licensing requirements vary by state. Homeopathic products are regulated by the FDA, but no uniform prescribing standards exist.

🐍
Asclepius & Hygeia: Deities of Medicine

Asclepius, born of Apollo and the mortal Coronis, was both hero and god of medicine in Greek mythology. His descendants, the Asclepiades, included Hygeia, goddess of health and a companion of Aphrodite. Both deities are associated with the snake, a creature long regarded as magickal and symbolic of renewal through the shedding of its skin. Together they represent the dual nature of healing: maintaining ongoing health and seeking remedy when balance is lost.

Indigenous and Tribal Medicine

Indigenous healing traditions weave together herbs, minerals, animal medicine, and magickal practice into a unified approach to health. These systems are transmitted orally across generations, and each tradition is distinct, shaped by the specific land, culture, and spiritual worldview of the people who practice it.

Because these traditions are inseparable from their cultural and ceremonial context, they belong to the communities that hold them. They are not interchangeable or freely transferable to outside practitioners. Awareness of and respect for that boundary matters, particularly as certain practices have moved into mainstream wellness spaces.

⚠️
Practices such as smudging with sage and sweetgrass, or sweat lodge ceremonies, originate within specific Indigenous traditions and carry deep cultural and spiritual significance. These practices are sacred to their communities and should only be engaged in by those within those traditions, or with explicit guidance and permission from knowledge holders.

Aromatherapy

Aromatherapy uses medicinal-grade plant extracts, typically in the form of essential oils, diluted into carrier oils for topical application or, in some practices, internal use. It also works through direct inhalation, engaging the olfactory system to produce therapeutic and emotional effects. Aromatherapy bridges the practical and the magickal naturally, as scent is one of the most immediate ways plants communicate their properties.

Flower Essences

Developed by Dr. Edward Bach in the 1930s, flower essences contain trace amounts of plant material steeped in water and preserved with a small amount of alcohol. The philosophy underlying flower essences is that emotional wellbeing is the foundation of physical health. By stabilizing the emotional state, the body is given the conditions it needs to heal.

In the Bach system, specific flowers address specific emotional states: Gentian supports those feeling discouraged or low, Vervain helps those who are tense or overextended, Oak supports those who push themselves past their limits, and Pine addresses persistent guilt. Once emotional equilibrium is restored, healing follows naturally.

For the practicing witch, flower essences are particularly interesting as magickal tools. They function as gentle banishing preparations, clearing emotional blockages, and can be used both internally and topically within a ritual context.

What Is an Herbalist?

An herbalist is someone trained in the therapeutic use of plants for health and wellness. According to the American Herbalists Guild, formal training involves 1,600 hours of study at an herbal medicine school plus 400 clinical hours.

Herbalists generally take a whole-plant approach, working with herbs in their complete form rather than isolating individual compounds. This philosophy holds that the natural balance within a plant contributes to its healing effect. The synergy of a plant's full spectrum of constituents works differently than any single extracted ingredient, a view that aligns closely with how witches understand the inherent intelligence of the natural world.

Plant Grimoire

Herbal First Aid Kit

A well-stocked herbal first aid kit is one of the most practical expressions of plant-based living. It bridges the gap between the everyday demands of the body and the deeper work of building long-term wellness. Unlike a conventional medicine cabinet stocked with targeted pharmaceuticals, an herbal kit works with the body rather than overriding it, drawing on plants that have been trusted across generations and cultures. The herbs you choose will reflect your needs, your climate, the plants available to you, and how you relate to them.

Herbs used for medicinal purposes are generally organized into four categories, each defined by its potency, the length of time it can be used, and the kind of work it does in the body.

Tonic Herbs

Tonic herbs form the backbone of any long-term wellness practice. They are gentle enough to use daily over extended periods, typically six to nine months, without risk of accumulating harmful effects. Rather than targeting a specific ailment, tonics strengthen and balance the body's core systems: digestion, respiration, circulation, reproduction, and the endocrine system. They are nourishing in the same way that whole foods are nourishing, working slowly and cumulatively.

Think of tonics as the herbs you live with rather than the ones you reach for in a crisis. Basil supports digestion and carries a long history of both culinary and protective magickal use. Rosemary strengthens circulation and memory, and is one of the most versatile herbs in both kitchen and craft. Thyme is a natural antimicrobial, valuable for respiratory support and as a preservative in herbal preparations. Mint soothes the digestive tract, eases tension headaches, and cools inflammation.

Because tonics are so gentle, they pair well with other practices: taken as teas, added to food, kept in sachets, or incorporated into daily ritual.

Stimulating Herbs

Stimulating herbs operate at a higher level of potency and are used in short, focused courses rather than over sustained periods. They are the plants you turn to when something specific needs addressing: an active infection, significant inflammation, a fever that needs support, or a system that has become sluggish and needs a push to reset.

The strength that makes stimulants effective is also what makes them unsuitable for casual, indefinite use. They can overstimulate the body over time, deplete resources, or produce diminishing returns if used continuously. Short, intentional courses followed by rest periods are the appropriate approach.

Echinacea is one of the most widely recognized immune-stimulating herbs in Western practice, used at the first sign of illness to mobilize the body's defenses. Boneset has a long history in North American folk medicine as a remedy for deep bone aches and flu-like symptoms, and was considered a staple plant medicine by many Indigenous communities before it was adopted into settler herbalism.

A careful herbalist knows when to reach for a stimulant and when to step back. These herbs work best when used with intention and restraint.

Adaptogens

Adaptogens are among the most studied and most misunderstood categories in modern herbalism. Their defining characteristic is the ability to help the body regulate its own stress response. They do not sedate, stimulate, or suppress. They help the body find its way back to equilibrium when chronic stress, exhaustion, or irregular demands have knocked it off course.

The concept of adaptogens was developed in the mid-20th century by Soviet researchers studying plants that could help the body maintain performance under extreme conditions. But many of the plants now classified as adaptogens have histories in Ayurvedic, Traditional Chinese Medicine, and folk herbalism that predate that research by centuries.

Holy Basil, also known as Tulsi, is one of the most spiritually and medicinally significant plants in the Ayurvedic tradition. It calms the nervous system, supports adrenal health, and is considered a sacred plant in Hindu practice, associated with protection and divine presence. Rhodiola, native to cold mountain regions across Europe and Asia, supports mental clarity and physical endurance under stress. Ginseng is among the most widely used tonic and adaptogenic herbs in the world, with distinct varieties in Asian and North American traditions, each valued for vitality and longevity.

Adaptogens tend to work best when used consistently over time and when the underlying causes of stress are also being addressed. They are companions in balance, not substitutes for rest.

Alteratives

Alteratives are the herbs of gradual restoration. Their role is not to fight a specific condition but to quietly improve the body's overall functioning over time, supporting the organs responsible for filtering, circulating, and renewing. They were a cornerstone of traditional Western herbalism and are sometimes described as blood purifiers or tonics for the lymphatic system, though their effects are broader than those terms imply.

Alteratives are often chosen when something feels persistently off but no clear cause is present: recurring skin flares, sluggish digestion, persistent fatigue, or a general sense of depletion that doesn't resolve with rest. They are preventive by nature, building resilience before imbalance becomes illness.

Garlic is one of the oldest medicinal plants in recorded history, used across nearly every healing tradition on earth for its antimicrobial, cardiovascular, and immune-supporting properties. Red Clover is valued for its cleansing action and has been used in folk medicine for respiratory and skin conditions. Red Raspberry Leaf is a nutritive alterative particularly associated with reproductive health, rich in minerals and widely used as a uterine tonic.

Of the four categories, alteratives are perhaps the most aligned with the witchcraft ethic of working with long cycles. They are not fast remedies. They are commitments to the body.

Building Your Kit

A useful herbal first aid kit does not need to be large or expensive. It needs to be honest, which means knowing what each plant does, why you have it, and how to use it. Start with a few herbs you already have a relationship with, whether through cooking, ritual, or observation. Add to the kit as you learn more, as your practice deepens, and as you tend plants directly.

For those who grow their own herbs, the kit becomes an extension of the garden. For those who source dried herbs or tinctures, provenance and quality matter. Medicinal preparations should come from clean, ethically harvested sources, free of pesticides and additives.

Let the kit evolve. The body changes, the seasons change, and the plants available to you will shift over time. The most effective herbal first aid kit is not a fixed inventory but a living practice.

Ritual Herb Gathering

Witches follow the rhythm of the seasons in their practice. The witch's New Year opens at Samhain, the cross-quarter sabbat that honors the dead and announces the coming of winter. It is also the moment of the seed, when herbs draw their energy down from leaf to root. The seed falls to earth or is carried on the wind, settling into the cool, damp soil to sleep through the dark months and emerge again as Ostara arrives. From there, herbs grow toward their full power at Beltane and reach their peak potency at Litha, when blossom and leaf connect the practitioner to the living Wheel of the Year. The entire life cycle of the herb, from seed to harvest, mirrors the sacred seasonal cycle. Witches therefore approach the gathering, storage, and use of herbs as a ritual act.

The Gathering

Herb-gathering traditions are rich with folklore passed down through centuries of practice. Much of this lore has been revived by modern witches, druids, and neo-pagans, who bring renewed meaning to ancient customs. Just as you would ritually prepare the tools on your altar before casting a spell, the same care and intentionality should be brought to the tools you use for gathering.

Before heading out to forage or visit a market, take time to enter ritual space and set your intention. Envision the best possible outcome for the herbs you are seeking. What do you need for wellness? What spells or charms do you have in mind? Approaching the work with a clear purpose aligns your mind with the task ahead.

⚠️
Avoid using tools made of iron when gathering herbs. This is a longstanding taboo in many traditions, as iron is believed to interfere with the plant's energetic properties.

Tools for Wildcrafting

If you plan to forage for herbs in the wild, gather the following tools beforehand:

  • Illustrated botanical field reference (for identification)
  • Bolline (the white-handled knife used for practical magickal work)
  • Small scythe (also a ritual cutting tool)
  • Garden snips or small handheld shears
  • Trowel or root digger
  • Basket or small brown paper bags

Steps for Ritual Gathering

1. Ground yourself before you begin.

It is customary to dress in white when gathering herbs. Some witches go barefoot, walking directly upon the earth as an act of grounding. The physical contact with soil, root, and stone brings you close to the energy of the Great Mother who nurtures the plants you are seeking. Even a few minutes of standing barefoot on bare earth can reset your electromagnetic field and deepen your connection to the work. If walking barefoot is not possible, removing your shoes and standing still for a few moments is sufficient.

2. Identify before you cut.

Use an illustrated field guide, not photographs, for plant identification. Illustrations convey scale and detail in ways that photos often do not, reducing the risk of misidentification. Once you have confirmed what you are looking at, consider how much you truly need. Dried herbs degrade over time, so there is no benefit to gathering more than you can use within a year. Plan your quantities with shelf life in mind, particularly for tinctures and infused oils, which keep longer than loose dried material.

3. Take only what you need, and ask first.

Before cutting, pause and speak to the plant. Invite it into your sacred work. This is not merely ceremonial; it is a practice of respect and reciprocity that acknowledges the plant as a partner rather than a resource.

The Benefits of Grounding

The practice of grounding, also called earthing, is backed by research into the body's exchange of electrons with the earth's surface. Loss of this connection has been linked to pain, lethargy, and disrupted sleep. Regular direct contact with the ground may help neutralize free radicals in the body and support improved sleep patterns and reduced chronic discomfort.

For more on grounding as a magickal practice, see Grounding.

Plant Grimoire

Herbarium as an Herbal Grimoire

A magickal herbarium functions as a personal grimoire, serving as both a record and a guide to your hands-on experience with plant allies. Whether you wildcraft, grow your own herbs, or source them fresh, pressing and mounting specimens creates a tangible archive that outlasts photographs or drawings. A well-maintained herbarium can last for years and documents not just identification but your lived, working relationship with each plant. This project can be personal or collective, with covens compiling a shared volume of their combined knowledge.

Gathering Your Specimens

Supplies

  • Field notebook and pen
  • Camera
  • Garden snips, scissors, or shears
  • Clean sheets of paper
  • Heavy book (dictionary, textbook, or telephone book)
  • Gloves
  • Backpack

Process

  1. Go out into the field, or work in your garden, with all supplies in hand. For each specimen, note the date, time, and location in your notebook. Photograph the whole plant within its environment. Collect as much of the aerial portions as the current season allows: leaves, stem, flowers, and fruit. Because a plant's appearance shifts significantly across its life cycle, recording the date gives your entries context and accuracy.
  2. After cutting, layer the herbs between two clean sheets of paper and press them inside your heavy book. This begins the drying and pressing process. If you are foraging and handling unfamiliar plants, keep gloves on throughout. Continue collecting until you have a meaningful start to your collection.

Drying, Mounting, and Organizing

Additional Supplies

  • Data sheet template
  • 2 wood blocks (two-by-fours work well)
  • 2 bricks
  • Clear contact paper
  • Clear plastic sheet protectors
  • Three-ring binder

Process

  1. Back home, begin the work of identifying, labeling, and finishing the press. Handle everything carefully at this stage.
  2. Mark a corner of each drying sheet with a sequential letter. Fill out a matching data sheet for that specimen using the same letter as its identifier. Each data sheet should capture:
  • Type of herb
  • Date, time, and location gathered
  • Moon phase at time of gathering
  • Physical description at gathering
  • Uses and parts used
  1. Move the pressed herbs from the book and transfer them between two wood blocks, then weigh the blocks down with bricks to finish the pressing. A commercial flower press is an equally valid option. Budget up to a week for thorough drying.
  2. Once fully dried, transfer each specimen carefully onto clear contact paper, drying sheet included if it has not stained. Lay the contact paper over slowly and smooth out any air pockets. Trim the edges and slide the finished specimen into a sheet protector. This goes on the right-hand side of your binder. The left side holds a second sheet protector with the corresponding data sheet inside.

Organizing Your Herbarium

The binder format gives you full control over organization. Sort alphabetically, by elemental association, by magickal use, by season, or any other logic that supports your practice. Whichever system you choose, an herbarium ranks among the most meaningful grimoires a practitioner can build: a physical record of the plant world woven directly into your spiritual work.

Working with the Phases

Waxing Moon

The period from new to full moon is considered especially fertile for sowing seeds of above-ground crops and for repotting or transplanting. During this phase, plant energy and sap are believed to flow upward, supporting growth in plants that yield above the ground. The combined gravitational pull of the moon and sun at the new moon is also thought to draw underground water tables upward, helping plants absorb nutrients and moisture more readily.

Waning Moon

The full moon marks the peak of potency for harvesting plants intended for magickal use. As the cycle shifts into waning, sap and energy are believed to move downward, making this an ideal time for pruning (plants may heal more quickly with less stress), planting bulbs and root crops, and weeding. Harvesting root crops is best timed closer to the new moon, when energy has fully receded below the surface.

Fruitful Signs

The three water signs (Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces) and fixed earth sign Taurus are considered the most fertile. Capricorn and Libra are also fertile, though somewhat less so. When the moon moves through these signs, it is a favorable time to plant, bless seeds, and transplant.

  • Cancer: Plant leafy things, plant above ground fruit
  • Scorpio: Prune to encourage growth
  • Pisces: Plant root things
  • Taurus: Plant root crops
  • Capricorn: Prune to strengthen bulbs, roots, stalks growing
  • Libra: Plant flowers and vines

Barren Signs

All three fire signs (Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius) are considered barren, along with Gemini, Aquarius, and Virgo. These signs are less favorable for growth but well-suited to maintenance work: gathering, pruning, and removing weeds and pests.

  • Leo: Kill weeds and pests, cultivate and till
  • Gemini: Harvest herbs and roots
  • Virgo: Plow, till, weed
  • Sagittarius: Prune to stop growth

Plant Grimoire

Language of Flowers

The idea that a small posy could carry a hidden message, especially between lovers, first took root in the East, though the older notion of flowers as divine messengers stretches back even further. One early example is the legend of the Buddha's teachings drifting down from the sky as blossoms. This practice of assigning particular meanings to flowers is known as floriography, and those meanings do not always line up with a flower's more widely accepted symbolism.

Interest in the custom spread through Europe, and from there to America, after Lady Mary Wortley Montagu traveled to Turkey in 1718. In letters home she described a system in which flowers and everyday objects were used to communicate. A related tradition called hanakotoba also existed in Japan, where its pull was strong enough that even the famed Samurai embraced it, with families often adopting specific flowers as their crests much like heraldic coats of arms.

Flowers were far from the only objects used to send coded messages. Fruits and other foods, gemstones, plain pebbles, and even lumps of coal could all carry meaning. A Turkish love letter, then, was often less a written note than a parcel packed with a curious mix of items.

Still, it was flowers that most captured the imagination. By the nineteenth century the craze for cataloguing nearly everything had taken hold, and lists pairing flowers with their meanings began to circulate alongside several books exploring the idea. A standard dictionary of flower symbolism, published in England in 1879, became widely used on both sides of the Atlantic. The timing matched the Victorian passion for flowers perfectly, as newly explored lands yielded rare exotics raised in hothouses as status symbols. Fresh blooms were worn in lapels and hair like jewelry, and floral images decorated stationery, fabrics, and china.

Over time the language grew more elaborate. Certain arrangements carried meanings greater than the sum of their parts, and even the way a flower was offered mattered. Victorians took up the fashionable pastime of making tussie-mussies, small posies wrapped in lace and ribbon.

The lists of meanings were never uniform, and that ambiguity continues today, even as some associations have become universal. The red rose, for example, is recognized everywhere as a symbol of love. Meanings also keep shifting with use. The daffodil once stood for unrequited love yet now signals hope, having been adopted as an emblem by certain charities.

Plant Grimoire

Sourcing & Purchasing Herbs

Many magickal ingredients come from distant parts of the world. You cannot grow a sandalwood tree in most climates, and purchasing herbs does not lessen their power. The global herb trade makes otherwise unavailable plant materials accessible for magickal work.

Most larger cities have at least one herb shop or health food store stocking dried herbs. Online and mail-order suppliers offer botanicals from around the world.

Evaluating Essential Oils

Be cautious when buying essential oils. If someone claims a bottle is "real jasmine oil" at an extremely low price, it is almost certainly synthetic. Even products labeled "essential" are often laboratory creations rather than true plant extracts.

Price is a useful indicator. Most genuine essential oils sell for significantly more than synthetics. Chamomile, yarrow, cardamom, neroli, jasmine, and rose are among the costliest. If a price seems too good to be true, it probably is.

Synthetics have a long history in herbal practice, but true essential oils carry plant energy that synthetics cannot replicate.

Evaluating Dried Herbs

Many stores do not refresh their stock regularly, so the rosemary you buy may be years old. When selecting dried herbs, look for:

  • Bright colors rather than faded or dull appearance
  • Few stem pieces relative to leaves and flowers
  • Fresh, strong scent appropriate to the herb

Avoid herbs that are mostly stem, show discoloration, appear insect-damaged or moldy, or have little scent when they should be fragrant.

Mail ordering makes quality assessment harder. If a supplier sends inferior botanicals, do not order from them again. Remember that suppliers depend on growers, and obtaining top-quality herbs year-round can be difficult. Use what you can find while continuing to seek better sources.

History

Native to Africa, aloe's reputation as a healing plant spans thousands of years. It held sacred status in ancient Egypt, where it was depicted on temple walls and incorporated into religious symbolism. Cleopatra is said to have made it a staple of her beauty regimen, and Alexander the Great reportedly used it to treat injured soldiers in the field.

Characteristics

Aloe is a succulent with thick green or green-and-white variegated leaves edged with small spines. The leaves and the gel inside them are the most commonly used parts. The gel is widely applied to burns and skin irritations and appears in cosmetic products from shampoo to toothpaste. The plant is also edible, and its sap is known to soothe upset stomachs.

Magickal Properties

Gender: Feminine

Planet: Moon

Element: Water

Powers: Protection, Luck

Magickal Uses

The aloe, a popular house plant, is also protective. It guards against evil influences and prevents household accidents. In Africa the aloe is hung over houses and doors to drive away evil, as well as to bring good luck.

Aloe vera leaves, full of healing and soothing gel, are shaped like spears. Keep living aloe plants on the altar for spiritual protection, particularly when working with volatile entities or dangerous spirits.

In Mexico, large wreaths made of whole garlic bulbs strung on wire are festooned with pictures of saints, packets of magickal herbs, lodestones, rock salt, pine nuts as well as clumps of freshly cut aloe. These are hung up in the home for protection, luck, money, and so on.

Aloe vera flower remedy counters psychic depletion after a long illness or personal crisis. Add it to the bath or take it internally according to the manufacturer's instructions.

In funerary tradition, aloe vera planted at a gravesite is believed to soothe the deceased, ease feelings of loneliness or abandonment in the afterlife, and prevent the soul from longing for or clinging to the living.

Additional Notes

There are over five hundred cultivated aloe species that have reputed medical benefits, and more; however we are most interested in its reputation as a protection plant.

The watery flesh of this succulent aligns it with the energy of the Moon and the sign of Cancer. Think of it as washing away anything aligned against you.

The gel of the aloe may wash away the pain of burns, but the prickly leaves mean that it is fully able to protect itself and your emotional needs.

Safety Notes

Fresh: X. Dried: P, N Dh X. Use with caution, fresh aloe can be irritating to some individuals.

Beauty & Skincare

Aloe is one of the most widely applied botanical ingredients in skincare. Its cooling gel soothes overheated, irritated, or sun-stressed skin on contact. Topical preparations ease inflammation and support the skin's recovery from sun overexposure and minor burns.

Aloe Vera and Aloes Wood

Aloe vera, a native of Zanzibar, is used for healing and protective magick. Its name means "true aloe," given to set it apart from the aloes of the Bible, which is believed to be the Southeast Asian wood now known as Agarwood. The two plants both offer profound gifts but are far from identical.

Arnica is a perennial flowering herb in the Asteraceae family, native to the mountain meadows of North America and Europe. Its vivid orange-yellow blooms closely resemble those of a daisy.

Botanical Description

Arnica is a perennial alpine herb with a creeping underground stem that gives rise to a rosette of pale oval leaves. The flowering stem stands up to sixty centimetres tall and carries a single, bright yellow, daisy-like flower. The whole plant is notoriously difficult to cultivate. It is native to northern and central Europe and is also found growing wild in Russia, Scandinavia, and northern India, with most commercial oil production rooted in France, Belgium, and Germany.

Related Species

A related plant, Arnica cordifolia, along with other species of arnica, is used in North America, where the herb is known as mountain tobacco.

Folk Tradition

Applied externally, arnica stimulates the peripheral blood supply and is considered one of the best remedies for bruises and sprains. It helps relieve rheumatic pain and a range of painful or inflammatory skin conditions, so long as the skin is not broken. The herb is never taken internally because of its toxicity, so its place in the home medicine cabinet has always been the tincture or ointment.

History

Arnica came to the attention of European botanists and healers in the late sixteenth century. Native Americans had long incorporated the plant into their practices before that contact, using the entire plant down to the roots. Over time, European herbal tradition refined its use to focus primarily on the flowers, which were prepared as tinctures and topical remedies for bruising, muscle aches, and sprains.

Characteristics

A hardy perennial in the Asteraceae (daisy) family, arnica produces vivid orange-yellow flowers that closely resemble those of a daisy. It thrives in mountain meadows and grows natively across both North America and Europe. The plant is widely recognized for its healing properties, particularly when applied topically to bruises, muscle aches, and sprains.

Magickal Properties

Arnica carries strong associations with strength and vitality, qualities drawn from its connection to rugged mountain landscapes. In ancient Greek tradition, these high-altitude regions were home to the oreades, the mountain nymphs, and arnica can be used to invoke their power. It makes a fitting altar offering when seeking to draw in vitality, and can be carried in a sachet to cultivate inner strength and resilience.

Beauty & Skincare

Arnica is valued in herbal beauty practice for its ability to accelerate healing in the skin. Applied topically in diluted preparations, it addresses bruising, swelling, and surface trauma. It appears in homeopathic formulas and topical remedies supporting skin recovery.

Bay Laurel (Laurus nobilis) is an evergreen tree with aromatic leaves used extensively in cooking and magickal practices.

Characteristics

A handsome evergreen tree growing up to 20 metres high, with dark green glossy leaves and small black berries. Bay laurel is often cultivated as an ornamental shrub for its dense aromatic foliage. Native to the Mediterranean, it is now extensively cultivated for its leaves and berries across France, Spain, Italy, Morocco, the Balkans, China, Israel, Turkey, and Russia, with most essential oil production centered in the Balkans.

Related Species

Several unrelated trees share the common name "Bay" and are sometimes mistaken for true bay laurel. Californian Bay (Umbellularia californica) and West Indian Bay (Pimenta racemosa, the source of bay rum) yield very different oils. The Cherry Laurel (Prunus laurocerasus) shares the laurel name but is poisonous and should never be substituted for true bay in cooking, medicine, or ritual.

Lore & History

Bay laurel was used to fashion wreaths in ancient Greece that symbolized high status. These wreaths were originally given as prizes to athletes at the Pythian Games, but their use spread to victorious generals, poets, and musicians. The symbolism of victory and triumph carried over into Roman culture and persists today. "Laurel" is the source of the word laureate (someone who has received high honors for a creative or technical achievement) and the expression "to rest on one's laurels."

In the ancient world, bay laurel was particularly associated with the Greek sun god Apollo, who ruled over prophecy and trance. He presided over the Temple at Delphi, where his oracle (also called a pythia or sibyl) would fall into trance and deliver prophecy. Some ancient sources claim the oracle entered trance through the use of bay laurel, though it is unclear whether these sources were referring to the same plant known by that name today.

Ghost Magick

A wreath of fresh bay laurel leaves posted on entrance doors signals to ghosts that they are not welcome and may not enter.

Magickal Uses

Sacred to Apollo and the Sun, laurel garlands were given to poets, heroes, and others who excelled in courage, service, and the creation of beauty. The priestesses of the Triple Goddess and the Delphic oracles chewed the leaves for prophecy, and bay is used in clairvoyance and wisdom brews as well, though its taste is strong. Bay leaves placed beneath the pillow induce prophetic dreams, and burning them causes visions. The ancient priestesses also inhaled their fumes to induce a prophetic state, and bay leaves are used as decorations at Yule.

Bay is a protection and purification herb par excellence. Wearing it as an amulet wards off negativity and evil; burning or scattering it during exorcism rituals clears the space; placing it in windows protects against lightning; and hanging it up prevents poltergeists. Place at least one bay leaf in each corner of every room to create an aura of protection. A sprig of bay is used to sprinkle water during purification ceremonies. The tree planted near the home protects inhabitants against sickness, and bay leaves mixed with sandalwood burned together remove curses and evil spells. Bay is also used in love charms, perfumes, sachets, and incenses of power.

To ensure a love will stay, couples break off a twig from the tree and split it in two, each keeping a half. Bay leaves give strength to those engaged in wrestling and athletic sports if worn during competition. They are a symbol of immortality and counteract the negativity and restriction of Saturn's influence. Wishes written on bay leaves and then burned are said to come true, and a bay leaf held in the mouth wards off bad luck.

Daphnomancy

Bay laurel has a deep association with the Oracle of Delphi. The pythonesses of Delphi were said to deliver their prophecies with bay leaves clenched between their teeth, and the fumes they inhaled to induce visionary states were widely believed to contain bay laurel as a key component, though the full formula has never been identified. The oracle's association with bay runs even deeper through the myth of Daphne, a pythoness said to have been transformed into the very first bay laurel tree while fleeing Apollo. In this myth the tree offered Daphne an avenue of escape when she was fleeing rape.

A second oracular shrine, named for Daphne and located near Tarsus, received its oracles by dipping bay leaves or branches into a sacred spring. This shrine, set within celebrated groves, was an early target of Christian suppression. The practice of bay laurel divination, known as daphnomancy, survived independently.

To perform daphnomancy, hold bay leaves in your hand while concentrating on your question. Then either place a single leaf onto a glowing charcoal or toss several into an open flame. Leaves that crackle loudly and burn brightly signal a favorable outcome. Leaves that sputter, resist burning, or extinguish the flame signal that plans should be reconsidered or postponed. Flames that shoot cleanly and directly upward from the leaves indicate strong auspicious conditions.

Ancestor Veneration & Mediumship

Bay laurel is a popular choice for fumigations when working with the ancestors, especially during mediumship or divination sessions. The leaves smolder well and can be burned on their own. They can also be crushed and burned alongside frankincense, which shares bay laurel's solar attributes.

The dried leaves are large and flat enough that short petitions can be written on them. They are especially suited to petitions related to developing ability as a medium or diviner, or petitions addressed specifically to the ancestors.

The Greek Magical Papyri include several spells calling for bay laurel. In particular, PGM I. 262-347 describes creating a protective charm by tracing magical characters onto a seven-leafed sprig of laurel and invoking Apollo. This can be adapted by placing seven bay laurel leaves inscribed with magical symbols or petitions in an oil lamp and burning it during prayer.

Amulet Uses

A bay leaf carried as an amulet provides protection against spells and evil.

Folk Medicine

Both the leaves and the berries were once used for a wide range of afflictions, from hysteria and colic to indigestion and loss of appetite, as well as to promote menstruation and to bring down fever. Internal use has fallen out of favor due to bay's mildly narcotic properties, but a fixed oil expressed from the berries is still applied to sprains, bruises, and earache.

Culinary Uses

Bay leaves are a kitchen staple for flavoring soups and stews, infusing slow-cooked dishes with depth and warmth.

Moon Magick

Key themes for lunar workings: Protection, strength, prophecy, healing, purification, wisdom, success.

The Crown of Victory

The leaves that crown victorious leaders and great men are those of the bay laurel, the same tree that gives the kitchen its bay. Sacred to the Greek god Apollo, the laurel stands for the courage and wisdom that victory demands, and, like other evergreens, for longevity and immortality, all the more reason it was chosen for the victor's wreath. To chew or burn its leaves was said to grant second sight and prophecy, and so the oracular priestesses, the Pythonesses of Delphi, used it before they spoke their prophecies. In China too the laurel is a sign of immortality, and the sacred hare that lives in the Moon is said to pound its leaves into the drug that grants immortality to any bold enough to take it. The thought of fame and everlasting life lingers even in the tree's name, for Britain's Poet Laureate is named for the laurel.

Cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) is a perennial herb producing aromatic seed pods used as a spice. Known to pastry chefs as French cinnamon and "grains of paradise," this member of the ginger family has been used for centuries in both culinary and magical applications.

Characteristics

A tall, reed-like perennial herb growing up to 4 metres high, with long, silky, blade-shaped leaves. Long sheathing stems bear small yellowish flowers tipped with purple, followed by oblong red-brown seed pods. The whole plant is aromatic.

Origin & Distribution

Native to tropical Asia, especially the rain forests of southern India. Cultivated extensively in India, Sri Lanka, Laos, Guatemala, and El Salvador, with the bulk of essential oil production coming from India, Europe, Sri Lanka, and Guatemala.

Other Species

A family with many cousins. Round or Siam cardamom (Amomum cardamomum), found in India and China, is used as a local spice and folk medicine. A second oil is produced from wild cardamom (E. cardamomum var. major). Both are kin to Grains of Paradise (Aframomum melegueta) within the wider Zingiberaceae family.

Folk Medicine

Cardamom has been used in traditional Chinese and Indian medicine for over 3000 years, especially for pulmonary disease, fever, digestive complaints, and urinary trouble. Hippocrates recommended it for sciatica, coughs, abdominal pains, spasms, nervous disorders, retention of urine, and even bites from venomous creatures. It remains current in the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia as a specific remedy for flatulent dyspepsia.

Culinarily, it is one of the most-used spices of India, the Middle East, Latin America, and parts of Europe.

Magickal Properties

  • Gender: Feminine
  • Planet: Venus
  • Element: Water
  • Powers: Lust, fearlessness, purification, strength, focus, love, creativity

Historical Significance

The Ebers Papyrus (1550 BC), one of the oldest medical texts known to history, lists cardamom along with over 880 other medicinal herbs. In the realm of the magical, this spicy plant has been used in perfumes, incense, and fragrance for over three thousand years. It has been used to inflame passions and arouse lust, and has been added to wines as potent love potions.

Magickal Uses

For Lust and Love

The seeds are chewed to arouse lust, and are also used in love sachets and spells. Ground cardamom seeds are added to warm wine to make an effective lust potion.

Focus and Mental Clarity

Cardamom enhances concentration and helps quiet inner static. The seeds or essential oil can be used during test taking, planning, performing important tasks, and spell writing.

Self-Confidence and Success

Cardamom forges mettle and encourages bravery and self-confidence. It is especially useful when approaching love interests, making important sales pitches, or entering negotiations. Carry three cardamom pods in the right pocket during presentations or important meetings.

Bravery and Courage

Cardamom encourages the ability to stand on one's own two feet. It can be carried or used when facing difficult tasks that require courage.

Artistic Creativity

Venus rules not only love and lust but also beauty and the arts. Cardamom can be incorporated into artistic works to inspire creativity.

Prophecy, Divination, and Prediction

Burn cardamom pods over incense charcoal for prophecy and divination. Cardamom is traditionally associated with prediction and foreknowledge, making it an excellent addition to any divinatory working. This works especially well for divination regarding love interests or to know if someone has feelings for you.

Fire Elemental Magic

Cardamom has been used in elemental magic to evoke feelings of fire. It can be used when meditating on meeting fire elementals or working with salamanders.

Partnership Enhancement

To enhance a partnership, bless a pair of cardamom pods and have each person carry one in their right pocket or on their right side for three, seven, or nine days.

Conception and Fertility

Women trying to conceive can place a handful of cardamom pods into a muslin pouch to make a bath tea. The magical purification properties help increase the likelihood of conception, and the scent can arouse male partners.

Culinary Magic

In Arabic countries, cardamom was ground with coffee beans to warm the blood and make the heat more bearable, as it promotes sweating, while making the flavor more decadent. This practice combines the practical with the magical.

Moon Magick

Key themes for lunar workings: Love, sex, luck.

Cypress (Cupressus sempervirens) is a tall evergreen tree with slender branches and a statuesque conical shape. It bears small flowers and round, brownish-grey cones or nuts.

Origin & Distribution

Native to the eastern Mediterranean, cypress now grows wild in France, Italy, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, Spain, Portugal, North Africa, England, and to a lesser degree the Balkan countries. Cultivation and distillation usually take place in France, Spain, and Morocco.

Related Species

Many other species of cypress are found throughout the world and are used to produce essential oils, including C. lusitanica from Kenya. With regard to oil quality, C. sempervirens is considered superior.

Folk Tradition

Ancient civilizations valued cypress highly as both a medicine and an incense, and Tibetans still use it as a purification incense. It benefits the urinary system and is considered useful where there is excessive loss of fluid, such as heavy perspiration, menstrual loss, and diarrhoea. The cones were described as very drying and binding, good for stopping fluxes of all kinds. Chinese tradition considers the nuts very nutritious, beneficial for the liver and respiratory system, and helpful for checking profuse perspiration.

Magickal Uses

Symbols: Cypress symbolizes death, resurrection, and forgetfulness, and was often used in funerals.

Minoan cult: There was a sacred cypress cult in ancient Minoan culture that celebrated the mysteries of Hercules and his mother Aphrodite.

For consecration: Make a fire of cypress wood and consecrate ritual objects in its smoke.

For protection: Hang up a small bough of cypress for protection.

For lunar and seasonal incenses: Add cypress to incenses used during the waning moon or at the Winter Solstice.

For illumination on death: Carry cypress leaves to become illuminated concerning death in all its aspects.

The Tree of Eternal Life

Like all evergreens the cypress was taken as a symbol of eternal life, a fittingness made plain by the great age of many of its kind, for some have lived beyond five hundred years, and one standing by a Franciscan church near Rimini is said to have been planted by St. Francis of Assisi himself around the year 1200. Across most of the Mediterranean the cypress is the tree of funerals, yet it is also a hopeful sign of incorruptibility and of the resurrection of the soul. Its especially sweet scent deepens its sacred standing, and the fragrance drifting over graveyards was believed to purify the air. For that same purity and incorruptibility its wood is shaped into sacred objects, such as the shaku, the scepter borne by Shinto priests. In ancient Greece the cypress was a tree of the Underworld, and it was said that the first thing a soul met on entering the nether regions was a white cypress standing beside Lethe, the Fountain of Oblivion, whose waters washed away all memory before the soul was born again.

Meaning When Gifted

When cypress is gifted it carries the meaning of mourning.

Dill (Anethum graveolens) is an annual herb with feathery leaves and umbrella-like flower clusters.

Magickal Properties

Gender: Masculine

Planet: Mercury

Element: Fire

Powers: Protection, Money, Lust, Love

Magickal Uses

Against witchcraft: The dried ripe fruits were used by medieval magicians in spells and charms against witchcraft.

For home protection: Tie up the dried seed heads and hang them as protection for your home and property. Use the seeds in protection sachets and incenses.

Anise confusion: Some mistake dill for anise, whose flower cluster also has an umbrella shape. Anise, however, has a distinctively different odor.

Folk medicine — digestive cordial: Use the seed to make a cordial to relieve digestive problems, flatulence, headaches, and insomnia. In medieval times seeds were chewed to freshen the breath and allay hunger pains. Dill water was given to babies for colic.

For protection: Dill, when hung at the door, protects the home. It is also used in protection sachets, and when placed in the cradle, protects children.

For money: Use dill in money spells.

For love and lust: Add to love mixtures and food to cause lust. The smell of dill is said to stimulate lust.

To prevent hexes: No one can hex you when you carry a bag of dill over the heart.

Culinary Uses

Parts used: Seeds and feathery leaves

Dill brings good fortune and protective energy to the table. It is commonly used in soups, stews, and savory dishes.

Botanical Description

Dill is an annual or biennial herb up to 1 metre high with a smooth stem, feathery leaves, and umbels of yellowish flowers followed by flat small seeds.

Origin & Distribution

Native to the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions; now cultivated worldwide, especially in Europe, the USA, China, and India. Dill seed oil is mainly produced in Europe (France, Hungary, Germany, England, Spain); dill weed oil is mainly produced in the USA.

Related Species

Indian or East Indian dill (A. sowa) is widely cultivated in the east, especially in India and Japan. A commercial oil is produced from its seed which has a different chemical composition and contains 'dill apiol'.

Folk Tradition

Dill has been used since the earliest times as both a medicinal and culinary herb. In Germany and Scandinavia it is used with fish and cucumber, and the seeds baked in bread. In the west and east, dill is used as a soothing digestive aid for indigestion, wind, colic, and similar complaints, especially in children, a use still current in the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia.

Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus globulus) is a tall evergreen tree with aromatic leaves and distinctive peeling bark.

Magickal Properties

  • Gender: Feminine
  • Planet: Moon
  • Element: Water (source: Air)
  • Powers: Healing, Protection
  • Entities: Apollo, Thoth, Brigid

Folk Names

Blue Gum Tree, Stringy Bark Tree

Magickal Uses

For healing: The leaves are stuffed into healing poppets and small pillows and carried to maintain good health. The oil of the leaves is a powerful antiseptic that can be used to sterilize instruments. It also helps fight off colds and flu germs if burned in an aromatherapy vessel. Ring blue candles (existing entry says green — source says blue) with the leaves and burn for healing vibrations. To relieve colds, ring green candles with the pods and leaves and burn completely while visualizing the person as completely healthy.

For protection: The leaves and pods are also strung and hung around the house for protection, and the leaves carried for the same purpose.

For reversing harm: Eucalyptus has powerful reversing properties. Carry eucalyptus leaves in a reversing mojo bag (such as A Reversing Hand) to turn spells and harm back upon the sender. The leaves symbolically reverse the direction of negative energy.

As a protective amulet: String eucalyptus leaves and pods together and wear as a necklace or carry in a charm bag for protection against psychic attack and to reverse any harmful magick sent your way back to its source.

Botanical Information

  • Scientific name: Eucalyptus globulus var. globulus
  • Family: Myrtaceae
  • Type: Tree (leaf and flower used)
  • Height: up to 90 metres
  • Description: A tall evergreen. Young trees bear bluish-green oval leaves; mature trees develop long, narrow, yellowish leaves, creamy-white flowers, and a smooth pale-grey bark often coated in a white powdery bloom.

Distribution

Native to Tasmania and mainland Australia. Most commercial oil today is produced in Spain and Portugal, with additional cultivation in Brazil, California, Russia, and China. Very little oil now comes from its native range. Wood is also harvested for timber, especially in Spain.

Other Species

There are over 700 eucalyptus species, of which at least 500 yield an essential oil. Source-listed varieties fall into three broad chemical categories:

  • Medicinal (cineol-rich): Blue Gum (E. globulus), Blue Mallee (E. polybractea), Narrow-Leaved Peppermint (E. radiata var. australiana), Gully Gum (E. smithii).
  • Industrial (piperitone- and phellandrene-rich): Peppermint Eucalyptus (E. piperita), Grey Peppermint (E. radiata var. phellandra), Broad-Leaved Peppermint (E. dives var. Type).
  • Perfumery (citronellal-rich): Lemon-Scented Eucalyptus (E. citriodora).

Folk Medicine

A traditional household remedy across Australia. Leaves and oil are used for respiratory ailments such as bronchitis and croup, and dried leaves were smoked like tobacco for asthma. Also used for feverish conditions (malaria, typhoid, cholera) and skin problems including burns, ulcers, and wounds. Aqueous extracts are applied to aching joints, bacterial dysentery, ringworms, and tuberculosis. Both western and eastern herbal traditions employ it for similar reasons.

Therapeutic Actions

Analgesic, antineuralgic, antirheumatic, antiseptic, antispasmodic, antiviral, balsamic, cicatrisant, decongestant, deodorant, depurative, diuretic, expectorant, febrifuge, hypoglycaemic, parasiticide, prophylactic, rubefacient, stimulant, vermifuge, vulnerary.

Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare)

Symbolism

Fennel belongs to the element of fire and is sacred to the divinities who rule that element. Prometheus was said to have carried fire down from the Heavens to the Earth hidden in a fennel stalk, and the pith of the plant is held to be fireproof. Its fresh scent and sharp, reviving taste make it a symbol of rejuvenation, and to include fennel in a bouquet is to declare the recipient worthy of praise.

Magickal Uses

Grow fennel around the home for protection and hang it at windows and doors to prevent evil spirits and negative energies from entering. Carry the seeds for personal protection; fennel is one of the most versatile protective herbs, used in mojo bags to ward off harmful energies, spirits, and spells. Place a piece of fennel in the left shoe to prevent wood tick bites during outdoor activities. Add fennel to sachets and mixtures for cleansing spaces and promoting recovery from illness or spiritual attack. Hang fennel above doorways or sprinkle seeds across thresholds to prevent malevolent forces from crossing into the home. On Summer Solstice eve, hang fennel over doors to ward off evil spirits. Fennel is said to confer longevity, strength, and courage upon those who work with it. Stuff keyholes with fennel to prevent ghosts from entering a room; note that if a ghost is already inside when the keyhole is blocked, it may become trapped there.

Magickal Teas

Fennel can be brewed as a magickal tea to support healing, honor or invoke the Horned God, strengthen protection, and aid purification. Drink 1 to 2 cups only during the spell event itself.

Botanical Information

Foeniculum vulgare (Apiaceae / Umbelliferae family). Biennial or perennial herb, also classed as vegetable when the Florence variety is grown for its fleshy bulb. Grows up to 2 metres: a tall, upright herb with finely feathery leaves and clusters of small golden yellow flowers carried in flat umbels.

Distribution

Bitter fennel is native to the Mediterranean region and grows wild across France, Spain, Portugal, and North Africa, where the wild plants yield the "weed" oil. It is cultivated extensively worldwide, the main oil producers being Hungary, Bulgaria, Germany, France, Italy, and India. Sweet fennel is thought to have originated on the island of Malta, introduced by monks or crusaders thousands of years ago, and is now grown principally in France, Italy, and Greece.

Varieties

The two principal commercial varieties are bitter or common fennel (F. vulgare var. amara), slightly taller with less divided leaves and occurring both wild and cultivated, and sweet fennel (F. vulgare var. dulce), always cultivated and also called Roman, garden, or French fennel. Both are closely related to Florence fennel (F. azoricum), a smaller plant with a large cylindrical fleshy root eaten as a vegetable. Other named regional varieties include the German or Saxon, Russian, Indian, and Japanese fennels, each yielding slightly different oils.

Folk Medicine

A herb of ancient medical repute, traditionally believed to convey longevity, courage, and strength. It has been used to ward off evil spirits, strengthen the eyesight, and neutralise poisons. Both western and eastern herbalism prize it for obstructions of the liver, spleen, and gall bladder, and for digestive complaints including colic, indigestion, nausea, and flatulence; for the last reason it has long been an ingredient of children's gripe water. It has traditionally been used for obesity, possibly through a mild oestrogenic action that also increases the milk of nursing mothers. Still current in the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia, where it is used locally for conjunctivitis, blepharitis, and pharyngitis.

Therapeutic Actions

Aperitif, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antiseptic, antispasmodic, carminative, depurative, diuretic, emmenagogue, expectorant, galactagogue, laxative, orexigenic, circulatory stimulant, splenic, stomachic, tonic, and vermifuge.

Aphrodisiac Properties

The ancient Egyptians used fennel as a sexual stimulant. Fennel contains plant estrogens that help balance female hormones, which may account for its traditional association with fertility and desire.
